articles.title: Same price, less product: How to spot shrinkflation before you buy
articles.summary: Shrinkflation happens when companies reduce the size of their products without lowering prices. Here's how to spot shrinkflation and shop smarter.
articles.body:

Manufacturers are quietly reducing package sizes without lowering prices to match. Known as "shrinkflation," this trend means you could be paying more for less — even when the sticker price hasn't changed.

Between 2019 and 2024, for example, shrinking package sizes accounted for 3 percentage points of inflation in household paper products, 2.6 percentage points in snacks, and 2.3 percentage points in candy and chewing gum, according to a 2025 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO).

Here's how shrinkflation works, and how to fight back.

Shrinkflation is when a company reduces the size or amount of its product but continues charging the same price (or even raises it).

For example, say your favorite brand of cereal costs $4.99 for an 18-ounce box. The manufacturer reduces the box to 16 ounces but continues charging $4.99. Although the price hasn't changed, you're now paying about 12.5% more per ounce.

According to the GAO, some of the most common products affected by shrinkflation include paper towels, toilet paper, cereal, coffee, laundry detergent, toothpaste, and over-the-counter pain-relief medications.

The term "shrinkflation" is a play on the concept of inflation, but these aren't exactly the same thing.

Inflation is the sustained increase in prices for goods and services over time. In other words, you pay more for the same amount of a product as time goes on.

Shrinkflation is essentially a less obvious form of inflation. It occurs when manufacturers reduce the size or quantity of a product without proportionally lowering its price. This could look like fewer snacks in a multipack or more empty space inside a package.

Here's another example: Consider a bag of coffee that originally costs $10 for 20 ounces:

Inflation: The price increases to $12, but the bag still contains 20 ounces. You're now paying 60 cents per ounce instead of 50 cents.

Shrinkflation: The price stays at $10, but the bag shrinks to 16 ounces. You're now paying 62.5 cents per ounce instead of 50 cents.

In both cases, you end up paying more per ounce. However, shrinkflation can be harder to spot because the sticker price hasn't changed.

Further, experts say the effects of shrinkflation can disproportionately impact the most vulnerable shoppers. That's because shrinkflation commonly occurs with food-at-home staples (think: cereal, bread, eggs, milk, snacks). And those categories tend to make up a larger share of overall spending in lower-income households compared to higher-income households, according to Paul Stanley, Senior Economist at Numerator. "Based on this, shrinkflation's impact is often felt more by budget-constrained households," he said.

Customers are more likely to notice a price hike from their favorite brand than they are to notice a difference in quantity or units. In some cases, a shopper might see a price hike and decide to switch to a cheaper alternative or avoid purchasing that product altogether, which results in a lost sale for the company.

Instead, manufacturers reduce the size of the packaging — cutting their manufacturing costs in a way that can go virtually unnoticed by consumers — while still capturing sales.

"Brands often do this to diminish the public scrutiny that often comes with raising prices," Stanley said. "A smaller box is a quieter way to offset costs when inflation (and other macroeconomic factors) impact their bottom line." He added that it can also be simpler solution; adjusting sizing is a quick manufacturing change, while a price increase usually requires renegotiating with retailers.

How to keep shrinkflation from hurting your wallet

There is no federal mandate that requires manufacturers to be transparent about decreases in product sizes. However, several measures have been taken to promote pricing transparency.

Manufacturers commonly include product quantity information on their labels, and several states have implemented mandatory rules that require retailers to display unit pricing.

However, consumers still bear the bulk of the responsibility for spotting and navigating shrinkflation.

A few easy ways to identify shrinkflation at the grocery store and make sure you're getting the best value include:

Don't throw an item into your shopping cart based on the sticker price alone. Make sure you consider the cost-per-unit — AKA the cost per ounce, pound, or individual item — to determine which product actually offers the best value.

If your grocery store doesn't display unit prices, you can calculate it by dividing the total price by the quantity. For example, for a 16-ounce can of soup that costs $1.75, the unit price would be about 11 cents per ounce.

It's easy to overlook changes in the products you regularly purchase, especially when the packaging looks nearly identical. So, before repurchasing your household staples, take a moment to look for subtle changes in the sizing, such as fewer items in a multipack or fewer servings per package.

If you're unsure whether the packaging size has changed recently, you can compare the current size with previous purchases using old receipts or online order histories.

It's common for shoppers to stay loyal to a particular brand they like, but neglecting to explore alternative options could be driving up your grocery bill. According to Consumer Reports, "private label brands," or store brands, typically cost 25% to 30% less than their name-brand counterparts.

Of course, it's still important to compare per-unit prices even for generic brands — store brands aren't automatically the cheapest option.

Buying certain items in bulk can lower their per-unit price. For example, purchasing a 48-ounce container of laundry detergent may cost less per ounce than buying three 16-ounce bottles.

If you're worried about products going bad before you can use them up, focus on buying bulk non-perishables such as paper towels, toilet paper, and shelf-stable foods and condiments.

You might also consider becoming a member of a wholesale club, which typically offers the lowest per-unit prices when buying in bulk. Depending on your shopping habits, the potential savings can outweigh the cost of a membership.

articles.title: How much do you really need to save for retirement?
articles.summary: Figuring out how much you need to save for retirement can be tough, especially if it's still a long way off. These guidelines can help you determine the righ...

How much money do you really need to retire comfortably? The truth is, there's no one-size-fits-all retirement savings goal.

The amount you need depends on factors such as your desired lifestyle, expected expenses, retirement age, and other sources of income. A common rule of thumb is to aim for 10 to 12 times your annual salary by retirement, but your ideal savings target could be higher or lower. Here's how to figure out how much you'll actually need — and whether you're on track to get there.

5 common guidelines for estimating retirement savings needs

The following are some common strategies for determining your retirement savings needs. Use them as starting points when estimating your own retirement savings goal.

1. Save 10-12 times your annual income at retirement age

One of the most common guidelines for estimating your retirement savings goal is to multiply your annual income at retirement by 10 and 12, and use those numbers as goalposts for your nest egg.

Here's an example: Say you're earning $125,000 per year when you're ready to retire.

$125,000 × 10 = $1,250,000 $125,000 × 12 = $1,500,000

In this scenario, you'd aim to save between $1,250,000 and $1,500,000 for retirement.

The 25x rule is another popular method for estimating how much money you'll need to retire. It suggests saving 25 times the annual amount you'll need to withdraw from your retirement portfolio.

For example, if you expect to withdraw $40,000 per year from your savings, you'd need approximately $1 million saved to retire comfortably.

The 25x rule is based on the 4% withdrawal guideline, which suggests withdrawing 4% of your initial retirement portfolio in the first year and adjusting that dollar amount for inflation in subsequent years.

Here's how different annual withdrawal needs translate into retirement savings goals:

Keep in mind that the 4% guideline was developed around a roughly 30-year retirement. It doesn't guarantee your savings will last, especially if you retire early, experience poor investment returns, or face unexpectedly high expenses.

3. Calculate retirement savings needs by age

One way to track your retirement savings progress is to measure your nest egg against age-related benchmarks. These benchmarks aim to keep you on track as you save for retirement over the decades. They provide a measure of how much you should have stashed away as a function of your salary.

For example, if you're 50 years old, you should have 3.5 to 5.5 times your salary saved. So, if you earn $100,000 annually, that means you should have between $350,000 and $550,000 saved for retirement.

Different firms have published their own benchmarks over the years, but investment firm T. Rowe Price recently reevaluated these numbers. They're based on a retirement that starts at age 65. See the table below for a summary of this study's results:

Financial services firm Fidelity suggests that to have enough for retirement, you should save a minimum of 15% of your pre-tax income each year. (This includes any 401(k) match offered by your employer.)

For example, if your annual salary is $60,000 , you should be putting away at least $9,000 per year. If your salary increases to $90,000, you should save at least $13,500 per year.

The 15% rule comes from Fidelity's calculation that you'll need to generate about 45% of your retirement income from savings in retirement — the rest will come from Social Security .

This rule assumes continuous savings throughout your career from age 25 to age 67. So, if you get a late start or plan to retire at a younger age, you'll likely need to increase your savings rate to catch up on retirement savings .

The 80% rule says that you'll need about 80% of your pre-retirement income to live on each year during retirement. For example, if you earn $100,000 at the end of your career, you'll need about $80,000 annually to fund your retirement.

This rule is based on the idea that you'll have lower expenses in retirement. For example, you'll no longer set money aside for taxes and retirement contributions, and you may live in a paid-off house.

While the 80% rule offers a simple way to estimate your retirement budget, it doesn't give you a detailed picture, and it's based on several assumptions. For example, it assumes your lifestyle won't change in retirement. But if you plan to spend more on things like travel, giving, or healthcare, replacing 80% of your income may not be enough.

Factors that impact how much you need to save for retirement

These strategies are guidelines that are meant to get you in the ballpark of saving enough for retirement. But you should take these rules with a grain of salt, considering the following factors and how they'll affect your retirement needs.

Your retirement age plays an essential role in how much money you need to save. The earlier you retire, the more money you'll need to take care of yourself, and the less time you'll have for your money to grow. Plus, Social Security benefit amounts increase for every month you delay drawing them between the ages of 62 and 70.

How do you picture your lifestyle in retirement? Will you stick close to home and enjoy time with family and friends, jet off to see the world, or buy a second home at the beach? How you plan to live in retirement determines how much you'll spend each year, which directly correlates to the amount of money you'll need.

Though your health is hard to predict, it's worth thinking about when planning for retirement. For example, if you have a chronic illness or a family history of heart disease, you may want to plan for higher healthcare expenses in retirement.

Consider what fixed expenses you'll have in retirement. Will you still have a mortgage or other debt you're paying off? Or will you be completely debt-free? Similar to healthcare costs, it's hard to predict your fixed expenses decades into the future, but good estimates of these costs can help you better plan for retirement.

Ideally, you use a combination of retirement savings guidelines and your own personal circumstances to create a realistic goal. But if your savings pale in comparison to these guidelines or the average retirement savings by age , you can use the following tips to get back on track:

Create a retirement budget: It's tough to plan for retirement without knowing how much you'll need. Take the time to build a retirement budget by estimating how much you'll spend on various categories, such as housing, food, healthcare, and travel.

Earn your employer match: If your employer offers a 401(k) match, do everything you can to earn those dollars. It's essentially free money for your retirement savings stockpile.

Increase your contributions by 1%: Regardless of your age, start contributing what you can to your retirement savings. Then increase that contribution by 1% whenever possible — next month, next quarter, or even next year. The slight increase won't feel like much, but can make a big difference down the road.

Make catch-up contributions: If you're 50 or older, the IRS allows you to contribute a little extra toward your retirement accounts each year. As of 2026, those who meet the age requirements can contribute an additional $1,100 to their IRA and $8,000 to qualifying workplace plans.

Hire a financial advisor: Retirement planning isn't always straightforward, and you don't have to do it alone. If you're struggling to figure out how much you'll need or are concerned you're behind on saving, consider working with a financial advisor .

Saving for retirement isn't as simple as following a general guideline. Remember that the right amount to save for retirement is different for everyone, and the strategies mentioned are only suggestions. The key to saving for retirement is to start now, save consistently, and tailor your strategy to your unique circumstances.

Your savings account balance might be growing, but that doesn't necessarily mean it's gaining value. As inflation drives up the cost of everyday goods and services, it also chips away at your purchasing power.

Here's how inflation affects your savings — and how much interest you need to earn to keep up.

Inflation is the measure of how much prices increase over time, including the cost of basic necessities such as rent, utilities, groceries, and gas. As prices for goods and services rise, each dollar you've saved buys less than it did before.

That means even if your savings account balance stays the same, the actual value of your money is declining.

For example, let's say the inflation rate is 2% (which is considered a healthy rate of growth for the economy) and your savings account earns 1%. In this case, you're actually losing 1% of your wealth every year.

On the other hand, if the inflation rate is 2% and your savings account earns 4%, your savings are growing faster than inflation and your real return is 2%.

The interest rate your savings account needs to beat: 3.7%

Here's the bad news: We're currently experiencing a period of high inflation. As of September 2026, the inflation rate is 3.7% annually, largely thanks to rising energy prices.

So, if you want to simply preserve your purchasing power, you'll need to earn 3.7% APY on your savings. If you want to grow your wealth, you'll need to find an account that earns even more.

The good news? There are several banks and credit unions that offer high-yield savings options that beat inflation.

You're not likely to beat inflation if you deposit your savings at a major bank. According to the Federal Reserve, the national average rate on savings accounts is currently just 0.37%.

However, many community banks, credit unions, and online banks offer higher rates. Here are a few specific account types that are most likely to pay interest rates that beat inflation.

If your savings account needs an interest-rate upgrade, shop around for a high-yield savings account. HYSAs work just like other savings accounts, but they earn higher interest rates.

articles.title: VA disability checks could get bigger in 2027. Here's how much.
articles.summary: VA disability compensation COLA follows the Social Security adjustment. Here's what the 3.6% COLA in 2027 means for veterans.
articles.body:

Veterans receiving disability benefits are set to see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027.

Following the Social Security Administration's COLA increase this week, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is set to increase veterans' disability compensation by the same 3.6%. More than 6 million veterans who currently receive disability compensation from the VA will get the increase next year.

Each year, Congress must pass the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act before the VA can make the increase official. The law ties VA disability benefits to the Social Security COLA so beneficiaries can keep pace with inflation.

Now that the SSA has released the 3.6% COLA increase for 2027, the legislation must pass before the VA can make the increase official for beneficiaries. But veterans can still use the confirmed COLA to estimate how their payments will change.

Here's what to know about the 2027 COLA and how VA disability benefits will be affected:

The SSA announced on Oct. 14 that its 2027 COLA for beneficiaries is 3.6% — the largest increase in four years . The COLA amount is based on the Consumer Price Index for urban workers (CPI-W) averages for July, August, and September 2026, compared with the same months in 2025.

If Congress approves, the 3.6% COLA that Social Security beneficiaries receive will also apply to VA disability compensation.

VA disability payments are tax-free, and eligible veterans receive them monthly. Veterans can qualify based on mental or physical conditions that developed before, during, or after they served in the military. That might include conditions that appeared after serving, for example, or existing conditions that were worsened by their service.

Specifically, the COLA increase applies to compensation for wartime disability, compensation for dependents, clothing allowances for eligible disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation (DIC) for surviving spouses and children.

How much will the COLA increase VA benefits in 2027?

The VA hasn't published 2027 compensation benefits rate tables, but beneficiaries can use the current rate tables to estimate their COLA increase for the new year.

The monthly payment that eligible veterans will actually receive in 2027 depends on the specific benefits they qualify for.

For example, take a veteran with a 10% disability rating who currently receives $180.42 in disability compensation. That monthly payment will increase by $6.50 ($180.42 x 0.036) in 2027, for a new monthly total of $186.92.

The higher a veteran's disability compensation is, the more impact they'll see from the COLA increase.

A veteran with an 80% disability rating, for example, who also has one child and a spouse, currently receives $2,406.15 per month. In 2027, that monthly payment will increase by $86.62 ($2,406.15 x 0.036) for a new total of $2,492.77.

Beyond the amounts within the VA's rate table, a family's total VA disability compensation may also be affected by added amounts that they may qualify for. This includes additional children or Aid and Attendance benefits that spouses may receive.

For veterans receiving disability compensation, there's no action to take now.

The 3.6% COLA increase will automatically be applied to monthly payments throughout 2027. You don't need to file a new claim to receive it.

The Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026 — which will finalize the VA's compensation adjustment — has already been introduced into Congress, though it's still waiting to pass into law. Once it's final, the VA will update its current compensation benefits rate tables , and you can see exactly how your monthly payment is affected based on your disability rating and dependents.

The new rate should be effective as of Dec. 1, 2026, though based on payment dates, veterans aren't likely to see the increased amount in their disability compensation until Dec. 31 or even January.

articles.title: Yes, You’re Probably Paying More for Phone Service. Here’s Where Your Money Is Going
articles.summary: T-Mobile just raised a mandatory fee again, but it’s not the only carrier taking small bites out of your wallet.
articles.body:
Everything is getting more expensive bit by bit, and it's not just gas or grocery prices. T-Mobile just increased the price of a pair of fees that get added on top of what customers pay for their mobile phone plans , and it's not the only carrier doing this.

Over the past year and a half, the big three US cellular providers have raised prices in small ways that may not seem consequential month to month, but add up over the year.

For a while, a lot of carriers' plans rolled taxes and fees into them as a competitive advantage — when you know you're paying a fixed amount each month, it's easier to budget. Unfortunately, those days are over, at least among the big three US carriers: AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon.

The new fee increases are so small that you probably won't notice them on your bill. Effective Oct. 12, T-Mobile's Regulatory Programs and Telco Recovery fees increased for every line on a customer's account. For voice lines, it's an increase of $1.00 for the combined fees (previously $4.49 a month, now $5.49 a month). Mobile internet lines, such as those for smartwatches or tablets, went up $0.50, from $2.10 to $2.60 a month.

T-Mobile previously raised the cost of these fees in April 2025, from $3.49 to $3.99 and $1.40 to $1.60, so in a year and a half, customers are paying $2 more per voice line and $1 more per mobile internet line per month.

Even if your plan has a multi-year price guarantee, that applies to the main plan itself, not miscellaneous taxes and fees that are added on top of the plan's cost. Carriers can, and do, increase those fairly regularly.

For Roger Entner, analyst and founder of Recon Analytics, the problem isn't that carriers regularly raise fees like this. It's that they spread out the increases.

"I don't understand why they [don't] only piss you off once a year, but instead sometimes choose to piss you off four times a year," Entner said in a conversation with CNET. "It doesn't make sense unless you want to be hated."

T-Mobile isn't the only one that's increased these fees. AT&T raised its Administrative and Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee from $3.99 to $4.99 per line in August; that was after a December 2025 increase from $3.49. Verizon raised its fees in August 2025, from $3.50 to $3.78 per month for voice lines and from $1.60 to $3.97 per month for data-only lines.

As for the prices of the plans themselves, they've been relatively consistent. The exception is Verizon, which announced holiday deals in December 2025 and carried the pricing all the way through August when it announced the Simplicity plan . The myPlan plans, which include Unlimited Welcome, Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Ultimate, now cost $10 more per line for new customers than they did at the beginning of 2026.

articles.title: Vanguard economist says sticky inflation will test your patience
articles.summary: A top Vanguard voice says the inflation fight is shifting, and your monthly bills are in the crossfire.
articles.body:
Inflation rarely shows up as one big bill. It arrives as more of a slow leak in your monthly budget.

A fill-up costs a few dollars more. Your rent renewal lands higher than you planned.

For much of 2026, gasoline took the blame. The U.S. war with Iran pushed energy prices sharply higher, and many households assumed relief would come once oil settled.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate to a range of 3.75% to 4% on Sept. 16, its first hike since 2023, and it meets again on Oct. 27-28.

Now one of the biggest names in your 401(k) is telling you to look past the gas pump.

"The latest inflation report reinforces what we've been saying for several months: inflation is proving more persistent than many expected, particularly across services," Adam Schickling, senior economist at Vanguard, said in comments shared with TheStreet.

Energy still matters, but "the more important story is that demand has stayed remarkably resilient," he said.

Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September on a seasonally adjusted basis after a 0.4% gain in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics . Over the past 12 months, prices climbed 3.7%, up from 3.4%.

That topped the 3.6% annual rate economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected, Quartz reported, citing CNBC.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose 0.3% for a second straight month. The annual core rate climbed to 2.6% from 2.4%.

Here is where the September increases hit hardest, according to BLS data:

Gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month and 34.2% over the year, accounting for over half of the monthly increase.

Shelter rose 0.4% after a 0.3% gain in August and is up 3.2% from a year ago.

Airline fares climbed 1.2% in the month and 22.4% over 12 months.

Hotel and lodging prices rose 2% after a 2.4% jump in August.

Grocery prices fell 0.1% and are up just 1.8% over the year.

That last line matters. Your grocery cart is one of the few places giving you a break right now.

Why services inflation is the number to watch

Prices for services excluding energy rose 0.4% in September, up from 0.3% in August, BLS figures show. That category covers rent, insurance, travel, tuition and haircuts, the things you buy that a factory can't make cheaper.

In my read of the BLS table, September was the fastest monthly gain for services since April's 0.5%. The trend is also picking up speed.

articles.title: Eleições nos EUA: Consumo de carne vira arma entre candidatos | G1
articles.standfirst: Em estados com forte tradição pecuária, republicanos acusam adversários de serem contrários ao consumo de carne. Democratas reagem com vídeos de churrasco e críticas aos preços dos alimentos.
articles.summary: Republicanos usam o consumo de carne para atacar democratas, que agora comem churrasco em público para provar conexão com eleitores nas eleições dos EUA.
articles.body:
Imagem de carne bovina nos EUA — Foto: J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Nas eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos, a carne está no cardápio.

Democratas e republicanos discutem os preços altos e a guerra com o Irã, mas também disputam quem gosta mais de carne.

O exemplo mais recente veio nesta semana, no Mississippi, em que o candidato democrata ao Senado dos Estados Unidos, Scott Colom, divulgou um vídeo com um trecho da senadora republicana Cindy Hyde-Smith, atual ocupante do cargo, dizendo que, se os consumidores estão insatisfeitos com os altos preços da carne bovina, "há muitas outras opções de proteína para escolher".

O vídeo então corta para um homem preparando hambúrgueres na churrasqueira, que diz: "Escolher outra proteína? Eu prefiro escolher outro senador."

A disputa no Mississippi é um tanto incomum porque é o democrata quem está atacando a republicana por causa da carne bovina.

Em outras partes do país, os republicanos têm retratado os democratas como veganos ou contrários ao consumo de carne , tentando mostrar que eles estão culturalmente desconectados dos eleitores, são hostis às indústrias pecuárias locais ou simplesmente não são masculinos o suficiente.

No Texas, republicanos resgataram uma declaração de 2022 em que o democrata James Talarico, atual candidato ao Senado dos EUA, comemorava o fato de sua campanha eleitoral ter deixado de comprar carne e passado a adquirir apenas produtos veganos de estabelecimentos locais.

Desde então, Talarico tem aparecido publicamente comendo churrasco para rebater as acusações de que suas escolhas alimentares significam que ele não é um texano de verdade.

O candidato democrata ao Senado James Talarico discursa durante um comício em 13 de julho de 2026, em Eagle Pass, no Texas, Estados Unidos. — Foto: (Foto: AP/Brenda Bazán, Arquivo)

No Colorado , os republicanos têm atacado o candidato democrata ao Congresso Manny Rutinel por seu ativismo contra a produção de carne e a pecuária industrial. Na faculdade, ele foi fotografado sem camisa usando no peito uma faixa da organização Pessoas pelo Tratamento Ético dos Animais (PETA).

Em 2021, Rutinel fundou a Climate Refarm, organização que defendia a redução do consumo de carne. Ele também assinou cartas defendendo o aumento de impostos sobre carne e laticínios. Além disso, apoiou uma proposta submetida a votação em 2024 para proibir um abatedouro de cordeiros em Denver, que acabou fracassando.

Rutinel, de 31 anos, agora disputa uma vaga contra Gabe Evans, o republicano que representa o 8º distrito congressional do Colorado. A vasta região no nordeste do estado é pontilhada por ranchos, fazendas leiteiras e unidades de processamento de carne, incluindo a sede da gigante da carne bovina JBS Swift.

Os republicanos têm explorado intensamente o histórico de defesa do veganismo de Rutinel, a ponto de o grupo conservador de mídia Daily Wire divulgar nesta semana um vídeo gravado de forma oculta em que um integrante da campanha afirma que ele come carne "o mínimo possível".

Rutinel tem feito questão de aparecer em público comendo tacos de carne durante a campanha e conta com o apoio do sindicato dos trabalhadores da indústria frigorífica.

"Não acho que os moradores do Colorado se importem com o que está no meu prato", disse ele em entrevista após uma recente parada de campanha. "Acho que eles se importam mais em conseguir pagar pelo que está no prato deles."

Evans afirma que a questão vai além das preferências alimentares do adversário.

"Não me importo com o que ele come pessoalmente", disse Evans em entrevista. "Importa-me que ele queira usar o poder do governo para fazer todo mundo comer dessa forma."

articles.title: O que aconteceu com o experimento de Bukele para transformar El Salvador no 'país do bitcoin' | G1
articles.standfirst: Em 2021, El Salvador se tornou o primeiro país do mundo a adotar o bitcoin como moeda oficial. Hoje, boa parte do projeto foi abandonada diante da falta de interesse da população e da pressão do FMI.
articles.summary: Em 2021, El Salvador se tornou o primeiro país do mundo a adotar o bitcoin como moeda oficial. Hoje, boa parte do projeto foi abandonada diante da falta de interesse da população
articles.body:
O presidente de El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, prometeu que a adoção do bitcoin traria 'prosperidade, liberdade econômica e inclusão financeira' a El Salvador — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

"Em El Salvador, estamos começando a criar um país para o futuro, preservando o que nos torna únicos e buscando inspiração nas melhores ideias que já surgiram no mundo ao longo da história. E acredito que o bitcoin possa ser uma delas."

Foi o que disse o presidente Nayib Bukele em uma mensagem gravada e exibida durante a conferência Bitcoin 2021, realizada em março daquele ano, em Miami, na Flórida, nos Estados Unidos, diante de um público entusiasmado com a criptomoeda Bitcoin.

Na ocasião, Bukele anunciou que enviaria à Assembleia Legislativa um projeto de lei para fazer de El Salvador o primeiro país do mundo a adotar o bitcoin.

O anúncio foi recebido com uma salva de palmas pelo público, que via um antigo ideal prestes a se concretizar — e em setembro daquele ano, o país adotou o Bitcoin como moeda de curso legal no país (ao lado do dólar americano).

Cinco anos depois, o dólar voltou a ser a única moeda oficial de El Salvador, a aceitação do bitcoin passou a ser facultativa e a promessa de construir uma cidade futurista, abastecida pela energia geotérmica de um vulcão e dedicada à mineração da criptomoeda, nunca saiu do papel.

Afinal, o que restou do "país do bitcoin", como Bukele batizou El Salvador? O que foi cumprido do que se prometeu? E quem se beneficiou?

O que restou do projeto de transformar El Salvador no "país do bitcoin" cinco anos depois? — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

O bitcoin é basicamente um arquivo digital que existe online e funciona como uma moeda alternativa. Nisso, ele se diferencia muito de moedas convencionais, como o dólar americano.

Ele não é impresso por governos ou bancos tradicionais, mas criado por um processo computacional complexo conhecido como "mining" (mineração).

🔍 Todas as moedas e todas as transações feitas com elas ficam registradas na rede de internet – em um espaço conhecido como "blockchain", uma espécie de banco de dados descentralizado que usa criptografia para registrar as transações. Dessa forma, as transações não podem ser rastreadas.

E o bitcoin não tem um "valor inerente": seu preço é determinado pelo quanto as pessoas estão dispostas a pagar por ela.

A iniciativa de adotar o bitcoin em El Salvador começou em junho de 2021, quando a Assembleia Legislativa, controlada pelo partido do presidente, Novas Ideias, aprovou a lei que tornou a criptomoeda uma moeda oficial do país, ao lado do dólar — que já era a moeda oficial do país havia duas décadas.

A promessa era de que a medida traria "prosperidade, liberdade econômica e inclusão financeira".

O governo afirmava que o bitcoin reduziria os custos do envio de dinheiro por salvadorenhos que vivem no exterior, uma fonte de recursos que representa quase um quarto do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB, soma de todos os bens e serviços produzidos no país).

Em 2025, chegaram a 26,3% do PIB, segundo dados do Banco Central de Reserva de El Salvador.

A adoção da criptomoeda também facilitaria o acesso de trabalhadores informais sem conta bancária ao sistema financeiro e atrairia investimentos estrangeiros.

Para viabilizar a iniciativa, o governo criou um fundo de US$ 150 milhões (R$ 748 milhões) e ofereceu US$ 30 (R$ 150) a cada cidadão que instalasse a carteira digital Chivo no celular.

Também destinou outros US$ 50 milhões (R$ 249 milhões) à instalação de caixas eletrônicos e aos demais custos necessários para colocar o sistema em funcionamento.

O governo de El Salvador destinou US$ 50 milhões (R$ 249 milhões) à instalação de caixas eletrônicos para bitcoin e a outros custos de implementação do projeto — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

Nove meses depois, uma das primeiras pesquisas sobre a medida já mostrava o ceticismo dos salvadorenhos em relação ao bitcoin.

Entre os entrevistados pelo Instituto Universitário de Opinião Pública (Iudop), da Universidade Centro-Americana José Simeón Cañas (UCA), 71% afirmaram que a adoção da criptomoeda não havia trazido "nenhum benefício para a economia familiar".

O resultado reforçava as conclusões do Escritório Nacional de Pesquisas Econômicas (NBER, na sigla em inglês), uma organização americana privada sem fins lucrativos.

Em um relatório publicado em abril de 2022, a entidade constatou que a maioria das pessoas que instalaram a carteira digital Chivo deixou de usá-la depois de gastar o "bônus" oferecido pelo governo.

Bukele, por sua vez, continuou comprando bitcoin com dinheiro público, apesar dos alertas de especialistas sobre os riscos para as finanças do país. A preocupação era com a forte oscilação do preço da criptomoeda, que perdeu mais de 60% de seu valor em 2022.

"Às vezes, faço isso até quando estou no banheiro", escreveu Bukele em resposta às críticas na rede social então chamada Twitter (atual X).

Em janeiro de 2023, a Assembleia Legislativa deu mais um passo no plano de Bukele ao aprovar a inédita e controversa Lei de Emissão de Ativos Digitais, destinada a atrair investimentos estrangeiros.

Para convencer grandes investidores a apostar no projeto de adoção do bitcoin em El Salvador e conceder empréstimos de alto risco ao país, o governo anunciou no Twitter que a nova legislação abria caminho para a emissão dos chamados "títulos vulcão", que, segundo as autoridades, começariam a ser oferecidos em breve.

Era, talvez, a etapa mais ambiciosa do projeto. A proposta previa que El Salvador contraísse dívidas em bitcoin por meio da emissão de títulos no mercado internacional, como fazem os governos para captar recursos, mas, nesse caso, com lastro na criptomoeda.

Metade do dinheiro arrecadado seria usada para comprar mais bitcoin. A outra metade financiaria o início da construção da Bitcoin City (Cidade do Bitcoin, em tradução livre), uma cidade planejada aos pés do vulcão Conchagua, em El Salvador.

Imagem da maquete da 'Bitcoin City' divulgada por Bukele na rede social X — Foto: Nayib Bukele via Twitter

Para completar o projeto, a cidade futurista usaria a energia geotérmica do vulcão para abastecer os potentes sistemas de computadores responsáveis pela criação de novos bitcoins, processo conhecido como mineração.

"O plano é simples: enquanto o mundo mergulha na tirania, vamos criar um refúgio de liberdade", afirmou Bukele, em um discurso semelhante ao dos defensores mais fervorosos das criptomoedas.

Esse movimento tem forte presença nos EUA, onde o mercado de criptomoedas ganhou contornos ideológicos, impulsionado por republicanos radicais e anarcocapitalistas.

Esses grupos defendem o bitcoin como uma forma de reduzir o poder dos bancos centrais e a intervenção do Estado na economia. Também alimentam a expectativa de que qualquer pessoa possa enriquecer caso o preço da criptomoeda atinja valores exorbitantes.

Mas, afinal, o que saiu do papel entre as tantas promessas feitas para transformar El Salvador no "país do bitcoin"?

"Se considerarmos os motivos apresentados por Bukele para adotar o bitcoin, não há dúvida de que o projeto fracassou", afirmou o economista Carlos Acevedo, ex-presidente do Banco Central de Reserva de El Salvador, em entrevista à BBC News Mundo, serviço em espanhol da BBC.

"É evidente que o governo esperava que, a esta altura, toda a população estivesse usando bitcoin. A aprovação da lei, a criação do fundo fiduciário, toda a estrutura foi pensada para isso, embora pesquisas anteriores já mostrassem que a população desconfiava muito dessa experiência", explicou Acevedo. "E, nesse sentido, de fato, não deu certo."

Em 2022, quando o entusiasmo com a iniciativa estava no auge, uma pesquisa da CID-Gallup constatou que apenas 1 em cada 5 empresas aceitava bitcoin e que somente 5% dos pagamentos de impostos eram feitos com a criptomoeda.

Dois anos depois, em 2024, a BBC News Mundo constatou, durante uma visita ao país, que o uso do bitcoin era raro e se concentrava principalmente na região conhecida como Bitcoin Beach (Praia do Bitcoin, em tradução livre), nos arredores da praia de El Zonte.

O bitcoin "não teve a adesão que esperávamos", admitiu o próprio Bukele em entrevista à revista Time, publicada em agosto daquele ano.

Uma pesquisa divulgada em janeiro de 2025 pelo Iudop confirmou a baixa adesão: 91,8% dos salvadorenhos disseram não ter usado a criptomoeda no ano anterior. Desse grupo, 76,2% afirmaram nunca ter utilizado bitcoin.

Embora El Salvador tenha registrado um avanço importante no acesso a serviços bancários no ano passado, apenas quatro em cada dez salvadorenhos com mais de 15 anos têm conta bancária, segundo a pesquisa Global Findex 2025, do Banco Mundial.

A adoção do bitcoin também teve pouco impacto sobre as remessas enviadas por salvadorenhos que vivem no exterior.

Segundo os dados oficiais mais recentes do Banco Central de Reserva de El Salvador, o valor enviado por meio de carteiras digitais de criptomoedas entre janeiro e abril de 2026 cresceu 44,3% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, chegando a US$ 23,1 milhões .

Ainda assim, representou apenas 0,7% dos US$ 3,286 bilhões enviados ao país nesse período.

A maior parte do dinheiro enviado por salvadorenhos que vivem no exterior, essencial para o sustento de milhares de famílias no país, continua chegando pelos meios tradicionais.

"O problema é que a proposta partiu de um diagnóstico equivocado", afirmou Frank Muci, pesquisador da Escola de Políticas Públicas da London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE, no Reino Unido), em entrevista à BBC News Mundo.

"O que torna as remessas caras, com taxas elevadas, é, em parte, o fato de que o dinheiro é enviado em espécie nos EUA e os destinatários também querem recebê-lo em espécie", explicou o especialista, que já escreveu diversos trabalhos sobre a adoção do bitcoin em El Salvador.

Uma pesquisa da CID-Gallup já havia constatado, em 2022, que apenas uma em cada cinco empresas aceitava bitcoin — Foto: NurPhoto via Getty Images

Muci define o projeto como um grande nothing burger , expressão em inglês usada para descrever algo sem importância ou impacto significativo.

Sobre a suposta contribuição do bitcoin para atrair turistas ao país, como afirmam os defensores da criptomoeda, Muci considera que o efeito não é "significativo do ponto de vista macroeconômico".

"Se você me perguntar o que Bukele fez que realmente está transformando o turismo, eu diria que foi a política de segurança", afirma Muci.

Com sua "guerra contra as gangues", o governo Bukele conseguiu reduzir drasticamente a taxa de homicídios, ao mesmo tempo que transformou El Salvador em um dos países com as maiores taxas de encarceramento do mundo.

A queda acentuada da violência contribuiu para a reeleição de Bukele, em fevereiro de 2024, com uma vitória esmagadora: o presidente recebeu cerca de 90% dos votos.

Ao contrário da política de segurança, a adoção do bitcoin foi "uma medida que rendeu centenas de manchetes, se não milhares, mas que, no fundo, não teve resultado algum", prossegue Muci. "Além de gerar gastos com sua implementação e assustar os mercados, que durante algum tempo penalizaram duramente El Salvador."

"Embora o investimento não tenha dado o retorno esperado pelo governo, sua rentabilidade também não ficou muito distante da que poderia ter sido obtida no mercado se o dinheiro tivesse sido aplicado em outro ativo", afirma o economista Carlos Acevedo — Foto: Bloomberg via Getty Images

"Pelo menos é importante destacar que não houve perda de dinheiro", ressalta Acevedo, do Banco Central de Reserva, referindo-se aos bitcoins comprados pelo governo nos últimos anos.

"Embora o investimento não tenha dado o retorno esperado pelo governo, sua rentabilidade também não ficou muito distante da que poderia ter sido obtida no mercado se o dinheiro tivesse sido aplicado em outro ativo."

Até a última quinta-feira (8/10), El Salvador acumulava 7.798,37 bitcoins, avaliados em US$ 636 milhões (R$ 3,17 bilhões), valor que oscila conforme a cotação da criptomoeda, segundo o Escritório Nacional do Bitcoin, que divulga as transações em tempo real em seu site.

Mas os chamados "títulos vulcão" ainda não foram emitidos, e a construção da Bitcoin City também não avançou.

Samson Mow, diretor-executivo da JAN3, empresa de infraestrutura para bitcoin que ajudou a idealizar os "títulos vulcão", lamenta que os planos não tenham saído do papel.

"O lado positivo é que o governo manteve a legislação sobre ativos digitais. Com isso, criamos um setor regulamentado, próspero e sólido, que está crescendo muito rapidamente", afirmou Mow à BBC News Mundo.

Embora reconheça que não conversa com Bukele há muito tempo, Mow acredita que o presidente "ainda confia no bitcoin".

"Mas ele precisa conciliar essa convicção com as exigências de governar um país e com as pressões e condições impostas por uma instituição como o Fundo Monetário Internacional ( FMI ) para liberar uma grande quantidade de recursos para El Salvador", ressalta.

Em meio às dificuldades econômicas enfrentadas por El Salvador, o governo fechou, em dezembro de 2024, um acordo de financiamento de US$ 1,4 bilhão (R$ 6,98 bilhões) com o Fundo Monetário Internacional ( FMI ), sob a condição de "reduzir os riscos associados ao bitcoin".

No mês seguinte, sem grande divulgação por parte do governo, a Assembleia Legislativa aprovou mudanças na Lei do Bitcoin.

Com a alteração de seis artigos e a revogação de outros três, a criptomoeda deixou de ter curso legal. Seu uso ficou restrito a transações entre cidadãos e empresas privadas, e a aceitação, antes obrigatória, passou a ser voluntária.

Em setembro, o governo deu mais um passo para abandonar o plano original de transformar El Salvador no "país do bitcoin".

Durante a terceira avaliação do cumprimento das condições do empréstimo, cujo pagamento seria feito em parcelas, o governo transferiu "a participação majoritária e o controle" da carteira digital estatal Chivo para uma "empresa privada".

"A única coisa transferida foram as ações da Chivo, algo que já havia sido oferecido um ano e meio atrás, e não a reserva estratégica de bitcoin", escreveu Bukele na rede social X, depois que vários veículos de comunicação noticiaram a transferência.

"Aproveitem para ler como El Salvador conseguiu um superávit fiscal primário e superou todas as expectativas de crescimento econômico graças à segurança e à confiança dos investidores, além de ter alcançado uma redução significativa da pobreza, favorecida por melhorias na eficiência dos serviços públicos", acrescentou.

Somente na última quinta-feira foi divulgado que a empresa responsável pela operação é a Linguard Labs. Ainda não se sabe, porém, qual participação foi adquirida nem o valor da transação. O Estado salvadorenho continuará como acionista e sócio da empresa.

A parceria "público-privada" prevê o relançamento da carteira digital com novos serviços, entre eles transferências gratuitas de dinheiro dos EUA para determinados usuários, acesso a microcrédito, adiantamentos em dinheiro e pagamentos com diferentes ativos digitais.

O controle acionário da carteira digital Chivo passou para uma empresa privada, mas o governo de El Salvador continua como acionista e sócio — Foto: Bloomberg via Getty Images

O FMI também mencionou as compras de bitcoin feitas pelo governo salvadorenho no relatório em que autorizou a liberação de mais US$ 138 milhões (R$ 688 milhões) ao país.

O governo continuou comprando a criptomoeda mesmo depois de assinar o acordo de financiamento, embora a suspensão dessas aquisições fosse uma das condições expressas do empréstimo.

As operações constavam no site oficial do Escritório Nacional do Bitcoin, que divulga dados sobre as compras, as vendas e as reservas da criptomoeda.

Em comunicado, no entanto, o FMI afirmou que os bitcoins mais recentes haviam sido adquiridos por meio de "doações privadas, sem uso de recursos públicos", e que o governo salvadorenho havia se comprometido a não fazer novos investimentos.

"Não está prevista a aquisição de mais bitcoins além daqueles provenientes das doações documentadas", concluiu o FMI .

Mas quem fez essas doações? E qual foi o valor doado?

Essas perguntas se somam às dúvidas que cercam o projeto desde o início. Até hoje, não está claro de onde vêm os recursos nem quem fiscaliza sua utilização.

A BBC News Mundo enviou essas perguntas à Presidência de El Salvador, mas não obteve resposta. Também procurou o FMI , que informou não ter nada a acrescentar ao comunicado.

Embora reconheçam que o acordo com o FMI pôs fim às partes mais ambiciosas do projeto, tanto defensores quanto alguns críticos destacam sua importância simbólica.

"Foi importante para a ideia do 'país do bitcoin', de um mundo em que o bitcoin teria substituído o dinheiro tradicional emitido pelos governos", afirma Muci, da LSE.

Antes de 2021, a possibilidade de um governo adotar o bitcoin não passava de uma hipótese. El Salvador, sob o comando de Bukele, transformou essa ideia em realidade, ainda que apenas por algum tempo, destaca Mow, da JAN3.

"Para o bitcoin, serviu para validar a ideia. Já El Salvador ganhou visibilidade mundial", acrescenta.

Mow admite que esperava que outros países seguissem rapidamente o exemplo salvadorenho, mas afirma que a experiência mostrou que isso é "mais difícil do que parece".

"Mesmo quando um governo concentra muito poder, não consegue obrigar a população a adotar uma moeda", diz Mow, ao comentar as lições deixadas por El Salvador.

"Mesmo quando um governo concentra muito poder, não consegue obrigar a população a adotar uma moeda", diz Mow — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

"É preciso combinar medidas do governo que criem condições para o livre funcionamento dos mercados e eliminem as barreiras que dificultam a adoção dessa tecnologia com outras iniciativas voltadas à educação", avalia.

"De qualquer forma, não acredito que o bitcoin precise de uma lei que obrigue as pessoas a usá-lo. Estou convencido de que é a melhor forma de dinheiro que a humanidade já conheceu e de que sua adoção acontecerá naturalmente", conclui Mow.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Going by projections by global agencies, India is on course to surpass its 2003-2007 record of five consecutive years of 7% or higher growth,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Going by projections by global agencies, India is on course to surpass its 2003-2007 record of five consecutive years of 7% or higher growth, Kyunghoon Kim of Korea Institute for International Economic Policy said.Starting 2021, India has recorded a five-year average annual growth rate of 7.83%, marking the second-highest five-year average since 1960, Kim said in a social media post. Between 2003 and 2007, the economy had expanded at an average pace of 7.89%. “Sustaining such momentum over several years deserves attention,” Kim said.Following a 5.8% contraction during the pandemic, India’s economy rebounded sharply by 9.7% in 2021 and has sustained growth exceeding 7% in each subsequent year.After a 7.8% growth in the June quarter, most global outfits — from IMF and World Bank to OECD and rating agencies — have revised their projections to around 7% growth this year, making India the fastest growth major economy once again.Kim highlighted that the latest round of growth is on an expanded base as India’s GDP stood at over $1 trillion in 2007 and is now approaching $4 trillion. A 7% expansion now delivers larger absolute additions to national output. “It is projected to become the world’s third-largest economy around 2030,” he said.While structural and global headwinds remain, he noted that maintaining such sustained high-velocity growth across a population of 1.4 billion represents a milestone achievement. “I hope economists at major institutions and I will once again be adding a few decimal points to our forecasts when the next quarterly GDP figures arrive,” he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI is changing Asia’s jobs market: What it means for India
articles.summary: Asia has a tricky tightrope to walk as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes its job market: creating enough jobs for a growing workforce while ensuring
articles.body: Asia has a tricky tightrope to walk as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes its job market: creating enough jobs for a growing workforce while ensuring workers don’t get left behind as technology changes the rules of the game.The challenge is particularly significant for India, Indonesia and the Philippines, where expanding working-age populations need productive employment even as AI transforms industries expected to provide those jobs.The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 Regional Economic Outlook: Asia and Pacific points to a shift in employer demand since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. An analysis of approximately 40 million online job postings across 19 Asian economies found that demand for jobs more exposed to AI had declined by nearly 10 per cent compared with occupations less exposed to the technology.However, the trend does not suggest that AI is simply eliminating jobs. The report found that the decline in demand for workers in highly exposed occupations appears to have stabilised, despite significant advances in AI capabilities.Part of the changing employment landscape is being driven by demand for new technical skills. Prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation and AI agent development are among the areas creating new employment opportunities. Employers are looking for people who can put AI to practical use in business operations, integrate it into existing processes and improve productivity.Businesses using AI see stronger labour demandHow companies use the technology is emerging as an important factor in determining its employment impact. Around 6 per cent of firms in Asia explicitly seek AI skills in their job advertisements, according to the IMF report, highlighting the uneven pace of adoption across businesses.Firms that have adopted AI are seeing stronger growth in labour demand than those that have not. This pattern also holds for occupations highly exposed to automation, indicating that the technology can support human capabilities even as it reduces the demand for certain tasks.The employment effects of AI, therefore, vary according to how businesses incorporate it into their operations. Alongside the decline in demand for some AI-exposed occupations, the report identifies stronger labour demand growth among firms adopting the technology.Lower AI exposure may not be an advantage for India in the long runEmerging Asian economies, including India, may initially face less disruption because many workers are employed in agriculture and other sectors less exposed to AI. But this could create a longer-term difficulty if the technology makes it harder for workers to move into higher-productivity manufacturing and services.For countries with growing working-age populations, the challenge extends beyond protecting existing jobs. They must also create productive employment opportunities and enable workers to move into occupations that can support higher productivity.India, Indonesia and the Philippines will need to navigate these pressures as AI reshapes the sectors expected to employ their expanding workforces. The pace and effectiveness of adaptation by businesses, workers and economies will be crucial to how this transition unfolds.Skills and preparedness will shape the employment outlookThe IMF report places the emphasis on preparing workers and institutions for the changes ahead, rather than focusing solely on the adoption of AI. Education reform, reskilling, digital infrastructure and stronger labour-market institutions will be central to this effort.Businesses will need to invest in workers as they integrate AI into their operations. Governments, meanwhile, will have to prepare younger populations for changing skill requirements and evolving occupational opportunities.Asia’s ability to manage the transition will depend on how well it combines technological progress with workforce preparedness. Timely investment in skills could help the region use AI-driven changes to support productivity, innovation and sustainable employment, while keeping inclusive growth within reach.You use AI every day. articles.title: Refined in India, bound for West: Russian-crude fuel exports to Europe rise 43%
articles.summary: Russian crude is finding its way to Western markets through Indian refineries, with countries including the EU, Australia, the US and New Zealand buying
articles.body: Russian crude is finding its way to Western markets through Indian refineries, with countries including the EU, Australia, the US and New Zealand buying oil products worth 1 billion euros ($1.2 billion) in September.Refineries in India, Turkiye and Brunei shipped these products to sanctioned countries, with export values rising 43% since August, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).The EU was the biggest buyer of oil products from the three countries, importing shipments worth 667 million euros. Australia followed with 168 million euros, while the US bought products worth 154 million euros and New Zealand imported 19 million euros’ worth.CREA estimated that 295 million euros’ worth of the products exported had been refined from Russian crude.Jamnagar refinery leads exports to the WestIndia’s Reliance Industries-operated Jamnagar refinery in Gujarat supplied six of the seven cargoes unloaded at European Union ports in September, despite the bloc’s ban on oil products refined from Russian crude, which took effect in January 2026.Jamnagar also accounted for the largest share of the group’s exports to the US, with shipments worth 122 million euros. Russian crude made up 32% of the refinery’s crude imports between July and September.Of the seven shipments unloaded at EU ports in September, Italy received three, Romania two, and Spain and Cyprus one each.The value of exports reported as destined for EU ports from refineries processing Russian crude rose 80% during the month. These included a 104,000-tonne cargo of gasoil, or diesel, from Jamnagar that was still on its way to Rotterdam.EU ban on Russian crude products has a loopholeThe EU banned imports of oil products refined from Russian crude in January 2026. However, the restrictions exempt net crude exporters. CREA said this leaves a loophole because a country can export more crude than it imports while still processing Russian-origin oil at its refineries.The research group has recommended applying the ban at the refinery level. Under its proposal, oil products from any refinery that has processed Russian crude in the previous six months would be prohibited, regardless of the declared origin of the finished product.This is a recommendation by CREA, an advocacy group, and not existing policy.India's Russian crude imports fall 13% in SeptemberWhile exports of refined products to sanctioning countries rose, India’s imports of Russian crude fell 13% in September. This was the second consecutive monthly decline and the lowest level since April, CREA said.Imports dropped at all three of India’s largest importing refineries. Intake at Jamnagar fell 27% from August, while Indian Oil Corporation’s (IOC) Paradip refinery recorded a 21% decline. Nayara Energy’s Vadinar refinery saw imports fall 8%."Despite the decline, Vadinar overtook Jamnagar as India's largest importer of Russian crude."Smaller facilities also recorded lower imports. The HMEL Mundra Oil Terminal reduced its intake by 74%, while the Kochi refinery saw a 32% month-on-month decline.IOC’s Mundra Oil Terminal was the exception, receiving 570,000 tonnes of Russian crude in September after importing none in August."The main exception was the IOC Mundra Oil Terminal, which received 570 thousand tonnes of Russian crude in September after receiving none in August," CREA said.India spends 4.1 billion euros on Russian fossil fuelsDespite the monthly decline in crude purchases, India remained Russia’s second-largest buyer of fossil fuels in September, spending 4.1 billion euros on Russian hydrocarbons. China was the only country that bought more."India was the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in September 2026, importing a total of 4.1 billion euros of Russian hydrocarbons. Crude oil constituted 88 per cent of India's purchases, totalling 3.6 billion euros. Coal (309 million euros) and oil products (161 million euros) constituted the remainder of its monthly Russian imports," CREA said.Since December 2022, India has accounted for 37% of Russia’s crude exports, compared with China’s 50%.Why India turned to Russian oilIndia was a marginal buyer of Russian oil before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Its purchases increased after Western buyers pulled back and Russia began selling crude at steep discounts.Urals crude averaged $90.7 a barrel in September but continued to trade $23 below Brent crude. The discount remained unchanged from August.The decline in India’s Russian crude imports was not driven by US pressure alone, according to analysts at Kpler. Tighter supplies and stronger competition from China for Russian oil also contributed to the fall in volumes.Kpler expects India’s Russian crude imports to remain between 1.8 million and 1.9 million barrels per day in October.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Foreign investors have pulled Rs 52,100 crore out of Indian equities in October so far, taking their total withdrawals from the market in 2026
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Foreign investors have pulled Rs 52,100 crore out of Indian equities in October so far, taking their total withdrawals from the market in 2026 to Rs 3.12 lakh crore. The latest round of selling comes amid high crude oil prices, rising US bond yields and a stronger dollar, which have dampened investor sentiment towards domestic stocks.Data from the Central Depository Services Ltd (CDSL) showed that the October outflow followed withdrawals of Rs 35,861 crore in September. This marked a reversal from July and August, when foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) brought Rs 20,200 crore and Rs 29,631 crore, respectively, into Indian equities.The scale of selling this year has already far exceeded the withdrawals recorded in 2025. FPIs took out Rs 1.66 lakh crore from Indian equities during the whole of last year, compared with Rs 3.12 lakh crore so far in 2026, according to the data.Dheeraj Gaur, chief investment strategy officer at Choice Wealth, attributed the continued selling to elevated US bond yields, the stronger dollar and rising crude oil prices. Persistent US inflation has also raised expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike, increasing the appeal of US assets for foreign investors, he said.India is facing additional pressure from expensive crude oil, while the artificial intelligence-led rally in North Asian markets is attracting foreign money away from domestic equities, Gaur added.Brief buying offers little indication of a trend reversalForeign investors made a marginal return to buying on October 16, but the shift may be tactical rather than evidence of a lasting improvement in their outlook for Indian equities.V K Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments Ltd, pointed to two factors behind the temporary change: the US 10-year bond yield easing marginally from above 5.3 per cent to 5.08 per cent, and the rupee strengthening against the dollar.FPI activity also differed across sectors. Financial services and oil-related stocks continued to face selling pressure, whereas consumer services attracted foreign investment. This included digital platform companies, entertainment, restaurants and healthcare services, Vijayakumar said.Pabitro Mukherjee, deputy vice president-Research at Bajaj Broking, said the slowdown in FPI selling and the reversal in flows on Friday suggested that investor sentiment was stabilising. He cautioned, however, that high crude oil prices remained a risk to a potential recovery.Brent crude prices and developments in US-Iran relations will be among the key factors investors track in the coming period. In India, the focus will also be on second-quarter earnings for FY27, Mukherjee said.Foreign investors' selling extended to the debt market in September, although flows varied across investment routes. articles.title: Oil firms drop sugar-based ethanol from 2026-27 tender, cut maize price
articles.summary: The government is changing the way oil companies source ethanol for blending with petrol, with sugar-based raw materials being taken out of the latest
articles.body: The government is changing the way oil companies source ethanol for blending with petrol, with sugar-based raw materials being taken out of the latest procurement tender for 2026-27.State-run oil marketing companies (OMCs) will no longer buy ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses under the tender. The move is aimed at keeping more sugar available for domestic consumption while ensuring that the petrol-blending programme continues.Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd (BPCL), on behalf of OMCs, issued the tender on October 16, inviting bids for around 11 billion litres of ethanol for the period from November 2026 to October 2027. The requirement is linked to India's programme of blending 20% ethanol with petrol."The Government of India has issued directions that sugar diversion for ethanol be reduced to zero for ethanol supply year 2026-27," the tender document said, as cited by PTI. "No offers have been sought for ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar or sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses in this quantity bid tender," it added.What can oil companies buy instead?With sugar-based ethanol excluded, oil companies can source ethanol made from maize, broken rice, surplus rice procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and C-heavy molasses.However, maize-based ethanol producers will also receive a lower price. The procurement price has been cut from Rs 71.86 to Rs 68.86 per litre. The incentive paid for maize-based ethanol has also been reduced from Rs 5.79 to Rs 2.79 per litre.This means producers will have to work with a lower procurement price and incentive for maize-based ethanol, even as grain-based raw materials become more important for meeting the country's ethanol needs.Why has the government taken this step?The decision comes amid concerns over sugar supplies and rising prices. Poor rainfall in Maharashtra and Karnataka, two key sugar-producing states, has raised the risk of lower sugar output.India is the world's largest sugar consumer and has been using ethanol blending to reduce its dependence on imported crude oil. But sugarcane and sugar used to make fuel are also raw materials that can contribute to food supplies. When sugar production is under pressure, diverting them for ethanol can add to concerns over domestic availability.The government is therefore trying to balance the need for sugar at home with its efforts to reduce oil imports and emissions.Will petrol blending be affected?India has adopted petrol containing up to 20% ethanol, known as E20, as the nationwide standard. Ethanol is made from agricultural raw materials, including sugarcane and grains, and blended with petrol to replace part of the fossil fuel used by vehicles.The programme has also created a substantial market for domestic distilleries and given farmers an additional source of demand for their produce.The latest tender does not end ethanol blending. Instead, it changes the raw materials oil companies can buy ethanol from. With sugar-based ethanol excluded, grain-based production will become more important in meeting the requirement.The availability of raw materials, procurement prices and distillery capacity will be key to supplying enough ethanol during the 2026-27 supply year, which runs from November 2026 to October 2027.You use AI every day. articles.title: Even LinkedIn is getting tired of your AI-written posts
articles.summary: LinkedIn is upping its fight against generic, low-quality AI posts on its platform.
articles.body: Bland, AI-generated posts have made LinkedIn the butt of many an internet joke this year. The platform has heard its users’ complaints about lengthy, generic missives never touched by human hands loud and clear. As AI has made it easier than ever to create huge volumes of content cheaply and easily, that “slop” has flooded the internet. YouTube, Pinterest, Spotify and other platforms have all sought to limit the amount of spammy, AI-generated content their users see. But LinkedIn has been hit especially hard. Scrolling through the professional networking site earlier this year could mean being bombarded by bullet-pointed lists accented by emojis, references to “B2B sales,” and asks for a follow or comment for more. A report published in July by Pangram, a research firm that tracks AI content online, found that more than 40% of long-form posts on the platform were AI-generated, compared to around 30% on X and Medium and a smaller percentage on Reddit and Substack. So now, LinkedIn is upping its fight against slop. “I know you think you’re doing the right thing with your perfectly bulleted list and your hook at the top, and you followed all the advice from LinkedIn advisors across the internet,” LinkedIn Editor-in-Chief Dan Roth, who leads the platform’s content strategy, told CNN in an interview. “But what works is being human.” There is some irony in this, given that LinkedIn is owned by Microsoft. The tech giant has pushed for people to adopt its AI tools for everything from writing to coding, and it is up against steep competition from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. LinkedIn previously offered AI tools to edit or rewrite posts, although it recently scaled the offerings back. But low-quality AI posts are a business problem for LinkedIn. They all start to sound the same, Roth said. If users see too many generic AI posts, instead of content that really teaches them something or gives them a deeper understanding of a professional connection, LinkedIn risks losing them to other platforms. Fighting AI slop In August, LinkedIn rolled out a button letting users flag when a post “seems like AI slop,” which was clicked more than 1 million times within its first two weeks. Now, the company is trying to use its own AI systems to help weed out AI slop on the platform and to remind LinkedIn users how to post like humans. The company built a team largely made up of former journalists and social media experts who have an eye for recognizing generic, sloppy content. These experts help train LinkedIn’s AI model on what authentic, useful posts look like. If the model flags a post as low-quality, AI-generated content, it’ll be less likely to be distributed beyond that user’s direct connections. Also key to the strategy is a creator management team that acts as “content therapists” for executives, subject matter experts and other LinkedIn users, many of whom have gotten accustomed to the convenience of using AI to write what, on the surface, appear to be polished posts, Roth said. “A lot of times now today, they’ll run it through Claude or Gemini or wherever, they’ll post it on LinkedIn and it will perform poorly. And then they come to the team and they’re like, ‘Why did this do badly?’” Roth said. “And the best thing you can do is give it back to them and be like, ‘Did you enjoy reading this? Do you see yourself in this?” Instead, the team encourages users to embrace imperfection in their posts — to make videos by leaning a phone up against a coffee mug, rather than shooting in an expensive studio, or to dash off a post to start a conversation, even if it isn’t a complete thought. The efforts are showing early signs of success. Improvements to LinkedIn’s detection systems have resulted in a 40% decline in views of content classified as AI slop, the platform said last month. That’s not to say LinkedIn is entirely opposed to AI, Roth said, adding that “not everyone is a born communicator.” But failing to edit or personalize content means it’s less likely to reach a wide audience on the platform. “We just try to push people to be more human,” he said. “That is what is required to be able to cut through the noise.”

articles.title: FMCG firms feel the pinch: Will your favourite products cost more this Diwali?
articles.summary: The festive season may bring cheer to shoppers, but for FMCG companies, rising costs are turning out to be a bitter pill.
articles.body: The festive season may bring cheer to shoppers, but for FMCG companies, rising costs are turning out to be a bitter pill. With prices of key raw materials climbing, companies are struggling to protect their profit margins without making everyday products more expensive for consumers. The big question now is whether they can keep prices in check for much longer, especially in price-sensitive mass-market and rural segments.The pressure has increased in the September quarter, reversing some of the relief companies saw in the previous quarter. Firms absorbed part of the cost increase to keep products affordable during the festive season, but this has squeezed their margins.The rise in costs has not been the same across all commodities. Crude oil-linked materials, packaging, palm oil and sugar have emerged as major pressure points, said Naveen Malpani, Partner and Consumer Industry Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat."In rupee terms, palm oil prices were approximately 21 per cent higher year-on-year in September, while sugar prices remained around 18 per cent higher year-on-year despite correcting 8 per cent month-on-month," he said.Companies have not been able to make up for the higher costs through price increases and efficiency improvements alone, putting pressure on their operating margins, Malpani said."Pre-results analyst estimates projected operating-margin compression of approximately 45 basis points year-on-year across a group of major consumer staples companies, with some estimates indicating declines of up to 150 basis points for the companies covered," he said.For companies selling everyday products to mass-market consumers, raising prices sharply is not an easy option. Higher prices could make products less affordable, leaving companies to rely on cost-cutting, better procurement and carefully planned price changes to protect profits without hurting demand.“The sector should therefore prepare for continued margin pressure through H2, with recovery contingent on actual commodity movements rather than an assumption that the cost cycle has peaked,” Malpani added.Price hikes may have to wait until after the festive seasonFor now, FMCG companies are trying to absorb some of the cost shock rather than pass it all on to consumers.Parle Products Chief Marketing Officer Mayank Shah told PTI that rising inflation was a major concern for the FMCG industry and was “definitely worrisome”.However, companies are attempting to cushion the impact on their margins by improving efficiency and cutting costs instead of immediately increasing prices, he said.Demand remains robust across urban and rural India, Shah said, adding that companies had avoided passing on the entire increase in input costs to consumers.That could change after the festive season. Companies may consider raising prices depending on how agricultural commodity prices move and how the broader geopolitical situation unfolds.“Most decisions on price hikes would be taken only post festive season… So, you may see some sort of thing happening from December onwards,” Shah said.Companies are also looking at cutting discounts and advertising expenditure to manage their costs. However, keeping demand steady remains a priority, the executive told PTI.Food inflation keeps companies on their toesNestle India Chairman and Managing Director Manish Tiwary also acknowledged the challenge last week, saying "rising inflation, particularly food inflation" is a "reality".The company's commodity outlook suggests that cost pressures may not ease across the board in the near term. Coffee and wheat prices are expected to remain range-bound, while sugar and edible oils are likely to stabilise at elevated levels in the December quarter.Cocoa prices remain volatile because of weather-related crop concerns in key producing regions. Milk prices have strengthened seasonally but are expected to ease as flush supplies arrive, Nestle India said.This leaves FMCG companies facing a challenging second half of FY27. After the festive-season boost, the focus will shift to keeping consumers buying while trying to recover lost margins."Outlook for H2 FY27 remains cautious," said Malpani, adding, " Companies may continue to face cost pressures, with any meaningful margin recovery dependent on commodity prices easing and earlier pricing actions flowing through.The challenge is particularly significant for packaged foods, home and personal care products, and other categories that depend on edible oils, crude oil-linked materials and agricultural commodities.Apart from the cost of making products, companies must also consider how shoppers will react if prices rise. A price increase may help boost the value of sales, but that does not necessarily mean companies will sell more products.Consumers could cut back on purchases, switch to cheaper brands, opt for smaller packs or buy products less frequently. Any of these changes could limit the benefits companies hope to gain from raising prices.The outlook for food prices also carries some uncertainty. The potential strengthening of El Niño conditions during October-December could affect agricultural production and food prices. However, the impact on Indian agriculture will depend on broader ocean-atmosphere conditions and regional weather patterns. Higher food inflation is a risk, not a certainty.For rural markets, the combination of food inflation, incomes and weather conditions will be particularly important.“If food inflation rises or rural incomes weaken, consumers may trade down to lower-priced brands, choose smaller packs, reduce purchase frequency or defer discretionary purchases. The uneven monsoon and potential El Niño impact add uncertainty to rural purchasing power,” he said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: La situación económica en España no dista demasiado de la de nuestros vecinos europeos según los expertos económicos. De hecho, Niño Becerra ha usado sus redes sociales para hablar de una situación bastante repetitiva en distintos Estados. El experto financiero cree que los países están entrando en una contradicción. Mientras que la población acusa la subida de la inflación, los salarios permanecen inmóviles, los Estados continúan invirtiendo en Defensa o gasto de armamento. Una situación que, según Niño Becerra, sólo tiene un desenlace posible con el paso de los años. Para el experto financiero, sólo hay dos escenarios posibles para entender “los problemas para la población que pierde poder adquisitivo y que sufre la disminución y degradación de los servicios públicos mientras oye como los Estados quieren disparar el gasto en armamento o presienten quien acabará pagando la factura de la reconstrucción de UCR”. Esa deuda, actualmente, está estimada en 587 millones de dólares. En primer lugar, el primer contratiempo es que, por un lado, el capital ya no necesita comprar la paz social como durante la Guerra Fría y, por el otro, en que la población cada vez es menos necesaria para generar PIB. Para echar más leña al fuego, el catedrático de Economía defiende que “donde aún lo sigue siendo, los salarios son muy bajos debido a que la oferta de trabajo es menor que la demanda y la productividad es muy reducida”. Hay que tener en cuenta que las protestas por la vivienda o por el coste de la vida se han sucedido en las últimas semanas en España, Francia y Portugal.
