articles.title: Why We Can’t Solve the Affordability Crisis
articles.summary: Voters are fed up, but there is no quick fix.
articles.body:
If there's a constant in modern American political cycles, it's that voters are furious over affordability.

They were furious when inflation devoured their wages and Covid-era stimulus checks. They stayed furious when oil and gas prices rocketed following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. As prices ballooned — for houses, for cars, at the grocery store, at the doctor's office — their anger brought President Donald Trump back from the political wilderness.

Now, Trump is on the receiving end of that fury. Consumer sentiment is more depressed than when Wall Street melted down and joblessness soared following the 2008 financial crisis. Nearly three-quarters of Americans believe economic conditions are worsening, according to Gallup , and they identify rising living costs as the biggest impediment to their finances.

This next part is important, and it's also been a constant. Americans never stopped spending . They spent when their paychecks weren't keeping up with prices. They spent when high interest rates eroded their purchasing power. They spent when retailers hit them with tariff costs, and they spent through the longest government shutdown in history.

American paychecks are larger now than before the pandemic, even after five years of elevated inflation . When the Iran war pushed gas prices above $4 per gallon, people kept their wallets open. And when they claimed that rising prices had forced them to pull back, Federal Reserve researchers found they were actually buying more .

Voters are broadly dissatisfied with both the economy and the political leaders who brought us to this moment. It is foolish to say that anger is misplaced, or dismiss any sign of strain. But fury hasn't slowed consumption. And most people haven't been budgeting as if financial ruin is at hand.

Affordability is a political crisis. But right now, it's not an economic crisis. At the same time, millions of Americans really are struggling to get by amid deep structural issues in our economy. And that's not something that Trump or any elected official can solve easily.

"Economists find the word 'affordability' almost a nonsensical word," Betsey Stevenson, a former economic adviser to President Barack Obama and now a professor of public policy at the University of Michigan, told me.

It boils down to the fundamental elements of economics, she added. There are finite resources for meeting everyone's demands. Everyone's demands are different, everything comes at a cost, and "people always want more."

"You can afford anything," Stevenson said. "The question is just: What do you have to give up to get it?"

articles.title: Will Meta's earnings restore confidence in the AI boom?
articles.summary: Investor confidence in the companies driving the AI boom has taken a significant hit over the past week, with markets spooked by concerns that...
articles.body:
Investor confidence in the companies driving the AI boom has taken a significant hit over the past week, with markets spooked by concerns that the revenues delivered by the technology will not match expectations.

Chip giant Nvidia, a vital cog in the sector, lost more than $350bn in market value this week alone. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Sector fell more than 11 per cent during the week, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 down 5.5 per cent.

In that context, Meta's earnings after the closing bell in New York on Wednesday offer a big test of Wall Street's mood about AI before Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon all report the following week.

The AI-led rally that has underpinned the stock market in recent years has been driven by bumper earnings from the major tech groups. However, "there is now a lot of anxiety, especially coming into the election period" before the US midterms next month, said Venu Krishna, head of US equity strategy at Barclays.

Although Meta's revenue is expected to have risen above $63bn in the third quarter, analysts estimate that the pace of growth will have slowed and the tech giant's adjusted operating income will be lower than in both the previous quarter and the third quarter of 2025 at $18.8bn. Operating margin is also expected to have tightened to a little under 30 per cent, as costs from the Facebook owner's AI investments bite, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates.

"Earnings are so critical, especially this quarter. The bar is very high. Last quarter we saw that companies that missed got punished a lot and companies that beat only got modest upside," Krishna added. "It's unlikely you'll have the same kind of returns [this quarter] you saw in the last three years." Ramsay Hodgson

For the European Central Bank, the better than expected economic growth in the 21 countries that use the euro this year has been a mixed blessing.

The economy's surprising resilience in the face of surging energy costs, trade tensions and wider geopolitical uncertainty is positive for employment and strained public finances. However, with annual inflation at 3.8 per cent, almost twice the ECB's medium-term target of 2 per cent, stronger economic fundamentals may drive up inflation and could make an October interest rate rise more likely.

That is why next week's S&P Global Eurozone purchasing managers' indices — an important near-real-time gauge of economic activity — will be closely watched by analysts and traders. Economists polled by Reuters expect both the manufacturing and services indices to decline slightly to 52.5, comfortably above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction. This would represent a fall of 0.4 points in manufacturing and 0.5 points in services.
authors: Valentina Romei and Olaf Storbeck and Ramsay Hodgson

articles.title: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day
articles.summary: Inflation is reaching fewer corners of the economy. That doesn't mean life is getting cheaper.
articles.body:
Inflation is reaching fewer corners of the economy. That doesn't mean life is getting cheaper.

Only about 38% of the roughly 175 categories in the Consumer Price Index rose faster than a 3% annual pace over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. That's down from 56% in May and the fewest since spring 2025.

The count borrows a test from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who laid it out at Jackson Hole in August. He counts how many categories in the Fed's preferred PCE price gauge are rising faster than 3%, a gauge of how widespread inflation is. The Fed's goal is still 2%.

"Too many categories are still posting increases above 3% on both a six- and 12-month basis," Warsh said after the Fed raised rates in September .

By that yardstick, September looked better than its hotter-than-expected headline . The 12-month count slipped to about 47% from 51% in August. At the 2022 peak, about 4 in 5 categories topped 3%. In the two decades before the pandemic, about 1 in 3 typically did.

A narrower spread strengthens the case for waiting, and traders have leaned that way. The bond market put the odds of a hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 17% by Friday's close, according to Bloomberg data — down from roughly 33% after Wednesday's CPI report. Warsh declined to preview his next move in remarks Friday before the International Monetary Fund.

Some Fed officials want more evidence before moving. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called September's inflation report discouraging but told Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger he favors waiting before acting again . "We need to get more data," he said.

The holdout categories are the expensive ones

Electricity, rent, hospital services, and car repairs have all been rising faster than 3% over the past six months, after adjusting for seasonal swings. Gasoline is up about 34% from a year ago. Together, the categories still above the line make up at least 60% of the CPI basket, which the BLS weights by how much households spend on each item.

Groceries show the other side of the problem. Grocery prices rose less than 2% over the past year, yet they're still up nearly a third since December 2019. Electricity is up 43% over the same stretch.

Slower inflation means prices rise more slowly. It doesn't bring them back down, and the Fed has no intention of returning to 2019 prices.

Not everyone sees progress. "There is little evidence of a cooling or a broad-based disinflationary impulse," RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas wrote Wednesday , pointing to trade, energy, and AI as sources of stubborn price pressure. He expects another quarter-point hike in December.

articles.title: Why souring sentiment on CoreWeave should matter to investors
articles.summary: Breaking down what's happening to CoreWeave in two specific callouts.
articles.body:
While many have spent the better part of a month waxing poetic about the cool factor of Meta's ( META ) Muse AI agent and foaming at the mouth to get the latest read on Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) financials ( they were OK ), they have forgotten about the plumbing of the AI ecosystem.

And most importantly, how one little shift in thinking could unsettle said plumbing — sort of like if you try to flush a sneaker down the toilet.

I want to break down what's happening to CoreWeave ( CRWV ) in two specific callouts.

A lot of information is floating around on X and on Wall Street about what's going on here and what's not, and it's important you understand the connections.

Remember, the AI trade is very intertwined. How the market perceives the health of CoreWeave matters to how the market perceives the future financial potential of everyone from Meta to Micron ( MU ) to Sandisk ( SNDK ) and even to Amazon ( AMZN ).

I would add that perception is especially important now as hyperscalers are set to report earnings and find new sources of debt to fund their AI build-outs.

The first part is: What the hell is, in fact, going on?

CoreWeave's stock has been roasted this week , bringing its six-month plunge to 46%.

First, CoreWeave's corporate bonds across maturities continued to be dumped amid fears of an AI slowdown and its implications for the company's precarious balance sheet.

The rise in yields on CoreWeave's bonds even spurred Elon Musk to post "Yikes" on X in response to a post by venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya. You never want to see Musk say "yikes" on anything related to CoreWeave — or anything more broadly!

And second, in a new report, Gartner forecast that by 2030, "cost pressure and a lack of a differentiating business model will force over 80% of neocloud providers to cease independent operations."

CoreWeave is a neocloud. The report was essentially akin to yelling "fire" in a crowded theater.

The company sought to push back against the bears, telling me in a statement that it is confident in its funding.

CoreWeave was defended by several Wall Street firms — one being longtime tech analyst Tal Liani at BofA .

"This [move in CRWV] is more sentiment driven. This is not about fundamentals. This is not about them not being able to pay for the debt, et cetera. This is more sentiment driven and the sentiment needs to change. And what's going to happen is, as always, there's going to be a period of concern. And then the fundamentals will kick in, meaning revenues, revenue growth," Liani told me on Sozzi Unleashed , saying he stands by his aggressive $140 price target on the stock.

articles.title: Thirty seconds in Texas costs $12,000 as politics dominates TV
articles.summary: Buying a 30-second television ad in Harlingen, Texas, typically cost political candidates less than $500 two years ago. These days the spots are going for th...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Buying a 30-second television ad in Harlingen, Texas, typically cost political candidates less than $500 two years ago. These days the spots are going for the price of a serviceable used car in the small city near the Mexican border.

Last week, Democrat James Talarico's US Senate campaign shelled out $12,000 for a half-minute ad during a Major League Baseball game on the local Fox station. That's 26 times the cost of a similar commercial during the state's 2024 Senate race, according to Federal Communications Commission records.

And that's assuming a campaign can still get time. With Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton pouring unprecedented sums of money into the state, the candidates are struggling to book time on the air at all in places like Harlingen, according to GOP strategist Vinny Minchillo.

"You can't buy it," Minchillo said. "It's closed out."

It's a similar story around Texas, where Republicans and Democrats have poured more than $500 million into the state's Senate race. With early voting set to start Monday and a little more than two weeks to the election, the Paxton-Talarico contest is shaping up as one of the most expensive non-presidential contests ever as the two parties flood the airwaves and social media in a fight over a seat that could decide control of the Senate.

That spending is apparent every time a Texan turns on the television to watch a game or the news. The going rate for nightly news spots at a Houston NBC affiliate has almost doubled from 2024, and Paxton spent $60,000 for an ad on a Sunday Night Football broadcast scheduled for late October.

TikTok users are racking up hundreds of thousands of likes by poking fun at both sides' ubiquitous commercials. One omnipresent ad runs so frequently that it's turned a conservative activist from the Dallas area, Miriam Evans, into a familiar face.

The money is tilting towards Paxton, a conservative firebrand and Texas attorney general, fueled by an influx from the world's wealthiest person, Elon Musk. But Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative and seminarian, has amassed a formidable haul as well. He also has a slight edge in polling as he seeks to become the first Texas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1988.

articles.title: The $40-A-Barrel Cost Most Oil Consumers Never See
articles.summary: Soaring tanker rates are adding as much as $40 per barrel to oil costs, reshaping global trade flows and raising fuel costs for consumers.
articles.body:
When Americans think about the price of oil, they usually focus on the number quoted every day in financial markets. If Brent crude is trading above $100 a barrel or West Texas Intermediate is near $100, those numbers become shorthand for whether oil is expensive or cheap. But that market price is only part of what ultimately determines the cost of getting crude oil to a refinery.

But transportation has become a cost that has become impossible to ignore. Reuters recently reported that shipping roughly 2 million barrels of crude from the United States to Japan aboard a very large crude carrier could cost about $81 million. That works out to approximately $40.50 for every barrel on the ship, compared with roughly $9 million for a similar voyage a year earlier. At current rates, freight alone can represent a huge addition to the underlying value of the oil.

For most consumers, tanker rates are an obscure corner of the energy market. Yet the extraordinary increase in shipping costs is helping reshape global oil flows and adding another layer of expense to a market already dealing with elevated crude prices, refinery constraints, and geopolitical risk.

A barrel of crude oil is only useful if it can get from where it is produced to a refinery capable of processing it. The gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products produced there then have to make another journey to the markets where they are consumed.

In normal times, ocean transportation is inexpensive enough on a per-barrel basis that few consumers ever think about it. The largest crude carriers can move roughly 2 million barrels at a time, creating enormous economies of scale and allowing oil to travel halfway around the world without freight overwhelming the value of the cargo.

That system becomes far more expensive when tankers are scarce or voyages become riskier and longer. The Energy Information Administration says tanker rates reached record levels in September as insurance costs increased and ships took longer routes to avoid conflict zones. Longer voyages also tie vessels up for more days, effectively reducing the available tanker fleet even if the physical number of ships has not changed.

The distinction between the quoted price of crude and its delivered cost is therefore crucial. A refinery does not care only what a barrel costs at an export terminal. Freight, insurance, delays, and other transportation costs all become part of the economics by the time that barrel arrives.

articles.title: 'Just another scare': Wall Street sees the AI trade strong despite tech's latest rout
articles.summary: Wall Street still sees more gains for stocks heading into the end of the year.
articles.body:
Technology ( XLK ) took a hit this week as financing concerns mounted, dragging down key AI trade players and sending the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) and Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) into negative territory for the week.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and peer Nebius ( NBIS ) both closed out the week down more than 25%. Those companies along with Oracle ( ORCL ) are "probably at the bottom" of tech on free cash flow, noted Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson on Yahoo Finance last week.

Mortonson pointed to "a higher cost of capital" and "a lot of scrutiny now on circular finance."

Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang sought to ease concerns , expressing optimism about CoreWeave. Nvidia's backing is significant , given that the AI chip giant holds roughly a 10% stake in the neocloud provider.

Others on Wall Street echoed the sentiment.

" I see this is just another scare, right ? We had DeepSeek, we had tariff crash, we had AI death scare," Moor Insights & Strategy founder and chief analyst Patrick Moorhead told Yahoo Finance.

"Because the numbers are up so big on the AI trade, people are looking for a reason to sell as opposed to a reason to buy," he added.

Dan Ives, senior managing director at Wedbush Securities, called the sell-off the "same script, different cast," noting that CoreWeave exited the second quarter with a revenue backlog of roughly $104 billion, reflecting customer commitments already in place.

"We view this as AI infrastructure's SaaSpocalypse moment and expect the same outcome," he said, referring to the software sell-off earlier this year sparked by fears of AI-driven disruption.

Meanwhile, commentary from chip equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) and contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. ( TSM ) pointed to robust AI demand.

UBS strategists characterized the latest bout of volatility as more of a "recalibration of expectations" than a fundamental break in the AI investment story.

"We suggest investors focus on where AI spending is translating into sustainable earnings growth and broader enterprise and consumer adoption," wrote Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer of Americas and global head of equities at UBS.

Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

articles.summary: Talent500 survey of 2,000 Indian tech pros finds 71% want hands-on AI training but only 29% get it; 69% prefer GCCs and 79% may reject unclear career paths.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Indian technology professionals are increasingly looking for employers that offer hands-on artificial intelligence (AI) experience and clearly defined career paths, while multinational global capability centres (GCCs) are emerging as the preferred next career move for many, according to a Talent500 survey. Talent500 is part of ANSR, which has set up more than 200 GCCs in India.The survey of 2,000 technology, product and data professionals found that 71% wanted hands-on AI upskilling, but only 29% said their employers provided it. Career growth was another major concern: 87% said clearly defined career paths were very important when evaluating an employer, while 79% said they would abandon an application or decline an offer if growth opportunities were unclear. Overall, 80% said a defined career path would influence their decision to accept an offer.The gap is also visible in employees’ current workplaces. Only 46% of respondents described their career paths as very clear. Among GCC employees, the figure fell to 36%, compared with 50% in IT services and 51% in startups. This could make career clarity a differentiator for GCCs competing for experienced technology talent, particularly as candidates increasingly seek clarity on career progression before joining an employer.Nearly 59% of respondents said they were actively looking for their next role. Only 18% said they would definitely or probably stay with their current employer if a comparable offer came along. Among professionals with more than 12 years of experience, 91% would consider a move, compared with 72% of those with less than three years of experience.GCCs were the first choice for the next career move for 69% of respondents, ahead of Indian product companies at 37% and IT services and outsourcing firms at 28%. Career growth was the leading factor in evaluating a GCC, cited by 48%, followed by the global parent brand at 41%, India-centre leadership and culture at 36%, and exposure to AI and technology at 33%.The findings come as GCC hiring continues to expand, with demand increasingly shifting towards specialised AI, data and engineering roles. Vikram Ahuja, co-founder of ANSR and CEO of 1Wrk, said GCC hiring was growing 15-18% annually, with roles changing rather than hiring coming to a halt.“Companies have spent around $300 billion on AI tools, infrastructure and transformation over the past four years, but fewer than 6% of global companies report a positive EBITDA impact,” Ahuja said. He expects AI’s impact to become more visible at scale over the next 18 months.Demand is rising for data engineering, data science, specialised AI teams and professionals who can redesign business processes.Ahuja also sees growing relevance for forward-deployed engineers (FDEs), who combine engineering or product skills with business understanding to deploy AI in complex workflows. GCCs are well placed to build such teams because business functions and technology teams often operate together. He estimates that 10-15% of the engineering workforce in GCCs could qualify for FDE roles, although only a subset is ready today.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US says Europe refused to join push for tariffs on India, China over Russian oil
articles.summary: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on India and China for
articles.body: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on India and China for purchasing Russian oil, questioning why the United States should bear the burden of pressuring Moscow alone.Speaking to NBC News' Meet the Press on Sunday, Bessent said the Trump administration had approached European allies in the spring to seek coordinated action against countries buying Russian energy.“So we have asked—in the spring, I asked our European allies to join us in putting secondary tariffs on China, on India. They refused. So why should the US bear the burden?” Bessent said.He added that Washington could re-engage with its European partners, reiterating that President Donald Trump wanted to end the Russia-Ukraine war.“President Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop. And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation,” Bessent said.US defends 60-day pause on sanctions legislationBessent's remarks came after Trump temporarily waived certain provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving his administration 60 days to assess the potential consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs.Defending the decision, Bessent insisted that the administration had not lifted sanctions on Russia.“No sanctions were lifted on Friday,” he told NBC's Meet the Press, referring to Trump's executive order granting the waiver.The legislation, which received strong bipartisan support in Congress, provides for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.Bessent said the pause would allow the administration to evaluate the situation before deciding on further measures. He also defended Trump's record on Russia, citing sanctions imposed on Russian energy companies Rosneft and Lukoil.“President Trump sanctioned the two largest Russian energy companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, which dealt a catastrophic blow to the Russian energy industry,” he said. “So no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump.”US secretary of state Marco Rubio also defended the pause, saying the administration needed time to assess the consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs on the global and American economies.“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday.Rubio said the administration was also considering pressures on global energy supplies arising from the Iran war, attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine.Bessent accuses Europe of financing Russia's war effortBessent also criticised European countries for continuing to purchase Russian oil and gas while supporting Ukraine.Citing shipments from Russia's Yamal facility, he said 140 cargoes had left during the first six months of the year, with 136 going to European countries, including Belgium, Spain, France and the Netherlands.Those shipments were worth more than $8 billion, he said.“The Europeans have given Russia and Vladimir Putin more money than they've given the Ukrainians. They continue to gorge on Russian energy,” Bessent said.He added that the United States imported $4 billion worth of Russian products, including $1.8 billion in fertilisers, while European countries imported more than 10 times as much.Bessent also pointed to the UK's decision in May to waive its embargo on diesel and jet fuel made using Russian crude, questioning why similar criticism had not been directed at other countries.Rubio calls India an important allyRubio said Washington needed to consider the energy requirements of countries such as India before deciding whether to impose tariffs or sanctions.“These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others,” Rubio said.He added that countries such as India had diversified their energy supplies but could not immediately stop importing Russian energy.The comments came amid criticism of Trump's decision to pause enforcement of the sanctions legislation. Indian-American lawmakers Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam criticised the move, arguing that it weakened pressure on Russia and undermined Congress' authority.Bessent questioned over whether Ukraine is a US allyDuring the same NBC programme, Bessent was asked three times whether the United States considered Ukraine an ally. He did not give a direct yes-or-no answer.“We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” he said on the second occasion.Bessent said Washington supported Ukraine by providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing Nato countries to purchase American weapons for transfer to Kyiv.He also questioned why European members of Nato had not supplied Ukraine with more Patriot missile systems, arguing that they had the capability to do so.His comments followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's appearance on the programme, during which he warned that it would be a “historic mistake” for the United States to side with Russia.“We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions because I think that it's all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help the United States,” Zelensky said of Trump.Bessent criticised the Ukrainian president for publicly accusing Washington and Elon Musk of restricting resources used by Ukrainian forces. He called the allegations “very reckless”, according to NBC News.Bessent maintained that Trump wanted to end the war through a negotiated settlement, saying the conflict had to stop and that the president was working towards that outcome.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sylvester Stallone says 'Rocky' probably wouldn't get made today
articles.summary: The movie icon reflects on why a movie like 'Rocky' wouldn't get the green light today.
articles.body:
In today's ever-evolving media landscape, legendary actor Sylvester Stallone doesn't think a movie like "Rocky" — which was a big risk for the studio as it bet on a relatively unknown Stallone when it was made 50 years ago — would get greenlighted.

"People are looking for identifiable stories, simple stories. Where they're finding them now is on streaming, on 'Dateline,' on '20/20' — you know, real human interaction. But I don't think we're going to ever see them again in abundance, like 'Dog Day Afternoon' or Pacino kind of films, or 'Mean Streets,' or great films like 'The Lion in Winter' or 'Beckett.' It's sad, but it's true," Stallone said in a new episode of the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast (video above; listen in below).

"And I don't think the audience wants it either, because, you know, this generation doesn't have that same education that I had," he continued. "You know, the way schooling is, they don't teach the classics. They don't take poetry. You don't teach 'The Raven.' So it would be quite alien to them. I don't even know what they teach, but the one thing they do rely upon is complete and utter fantasy, escapism, which every young man, you know, they love that."

Stallone has earned his spot among Hollywood legends through blood, sweat, and tears.

With that success — ranging from big-screen films "Rocky" and "Rambo" to the series "Tulsa King," which returns for its latest season on Friday on streaming platform Paramount+ — has come an equally impressive business backdrop despite not owning the rights to "Rocky."

Recognizing the power of controlling his own IP, Stallone expanded his earnings beyond simple acting fees — which routinely topped $15 million to $20 million per project — by taking on writer, director, and executive producer roles across his iconic "Rocky," "Rambo," and "The Expendables" franchises.

In 2018, Stallone formed his own media operations, founding Balboa Productions, a film and television outfit that has successfully commercialized projects like "Tulsa King" and "Samaritan."

Stallone, 80, thinks Dwight Manfredi — his lead character on "Tulsa King" — will likely be the final big role of his iconic career.

"I think Dwight will take me into the sunset because that character is so ingrained in me," Stallone said.

The 10-year yield stands at 5.1%. On $1.1 million, that's about $56,000 a year. Add Social Security and total income is roughly $93,000. He spends $7,800 a month, or $93,600 a year. articles.title: Elon Musk’s ex says she turned down a $40M NDA — then her child support was cut to about $5M total. Was it all worth it?
articles.summary: That’s a roughly $35M gap over 21 years — and Ashley St. Clair says she’d make the same call again. In the new documentary ‘Musk,’ she lays out what the orig...
articles.body:
Ashley St. Clair says she was offered roughly $40 million to stay quiet about Elon Musk for good. She turned it down so she could tell her story.

In Musk , Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour documentary, the 28-year-old author and former conservative influencer describes what saying no cost her. The film premiered at the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 8 and expanded to theaters nationwide on Oct. 16, a day after Musk was in Texas showing off Tesla's new flying Roadster . St. Clair says the monthly child support she gets for their son, Romulus, now 2, fell to $20,000 — a fifth of the $100,000 a month she says Musk's team offered if she signed a nondisclosure agreement (NDA).

If the $20,000 rate held until Romulus turns 21, it would total about $5 million. By her account, the offer was worth about $40 million.

Musk, 55, denies ever making the offer. "She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims," he wrote on X on Sept. 9, replying to a TMZ post about her Venice comments.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

St. Clair first laid out the offer in a June interview with Don Lemon , which Moneywise covered at the time . She said it began when Musk messaged Jared Birchall, who runs Musk's family office, to "wire Ashley 15 million for a home and reserve capital." Birchall then told her there would need to be "some sort of NDA," she said.

In the film, she says the paperwork "was labeled as a child support agreement" and offered "a lump sum of $15 million and then $100,000 a month for 20 years." The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the offer in April 2025, said the monthly payments would run until Romulus turned 21. In exchange, St. Clair told Lemon she'd be barred from disparaging or speaking about Musk, his employees, or his affiliates "into eternity."

According to the Journal, the deal had no trust fund or life insurance for their son if Musk died before the boy turned 21, and St. Clair would have had to pay back the $15 million if she broke it.

St. Clair has said she couldn't sign it in good conscience and didn't want her son to grow up feeling like a secret.

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ becomes one of the biggest documentary releases in decades
articles.summary: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s genre-bending film about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes made more than $15 million in ticket sales.
articles.body: “You Can See Everything” just saw the biggest box office opening for a documentary in more than 20 years. Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s genre-bending film about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes made more than $15 million in ticket sales. Many weekend screenings in cities like New York and Los Angeles were sold out despite the three-hour running time. The film’s distributor, A24, called it “one of the largest limited-release openings of the 21st century.” “You Can See Everything” opened on fewer than 900 screens following a jaw-dropping surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival last month. Fielder and Oppenheim worked on the project in secret for years, filming with Holmes and her partner Billy Evans in the weeks before Holmes went to prison in 2023. Holmes was convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud Theranos investors, but she tried to convince the filmmakers of her innocence. Fielder, who appears on camera interviewing Holmes and Evans, takes the film in unexpected directions, thrilling critics and theatergoers. The film has an extraordinarily high 99% “fresh score” on Rotten Tomatoes and a record-high 4.8 rating on Letterboxd. The film “has rewritten the rules of documentaries as we know them,” CNN’s David Mack wrote in an opening-day article about why it “absolutely lives up to the hype.” Theatergoers clearly wanted to find out for themselves. “You Can See Everything” enjoyed the biggest opening for a film on fewer than 1,000 screens since “Borat” in 2006. It was the biggest non-music documentary since “Fahrenheit 9/11” in 2004. The other big documentary this year — Amazon MGM’s “Melania” film about the first lady — premiered on twice as many screens and made less than half as much money, $7.1 million, in its opening weekend. And “Melania” was considered a box-office success in documentary terms when it was released. “You Can See Everything” is in a category of its own. Some film critics have predicted it will receive a Best Picture nomination. It opens nationwide next weekend, sure to benefit from all the buzz from its opening weekend. Overall, “You Can See Everything” finished No. 2 at the weekend box office in North America. Paramount’s video game adaptation of “Street Fighter” topped the box office with an estimated $30 million in ticket sales from 3,575 screens. Paramount is owned by Skydance, which also owns CNN.

articles.title: Gold Edges Higher as Traders Ease Rate-Hike Bets on Warsh Speech
articles.summary: Gold opened the week higher as traders pared bets on the Federal Reserve raising interest rates this month after remarks by Chair Kevin Warsh.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Gold opened the week higher as traders pared bets on the Federal Reserve raising interest rates this month after remarks by Chair Kevin Warsh.

Bullion was trading around $4,180 an ounce, after falling 0.7% the week before. Traders unwound bets on the probability of a quarter-point hike to less than one-in-five after comments by the Fed chair were interpreted as supporting the case to keep rates on hold when it meets next week. Higher borrowing costs are a headwind for gold, which doesn't pay interest.

A hot US inflation print last week had spurred expectations for US hikes, boosting the dollar, but Warsh's comments halted its gains.

Gold has held above the key $4,000-an-ounce support threshold since August, with its status as a safe haven asset providing a floor since a war-driven slump pushed it into bear territory earlier this year. It is still down around a fifth since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February.

Spot gold rose 0.4% to $4,180.97 an ounce at 7:35 a.m. in Singapore, while silver gained 0.6% to $57.33. Platinum and palladium advanced. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was little changed after falling 0.3% last week.

articles.title: Bolsa Família 2026: pagamentos de outubro começam nesta segunda | G1
articles.standfirst: Governo elevou o pagamento mínimo do programa de R$ 600 para R$ 691 por família, além de ampliar os benefícios complementares.
articles.summary: Governo elevou o pagamento mínimo do programa de R$ 600 para R$ 691 por família, além de ampliar os benefícios complementares.
articles.body:
A Caixa Econômica Federal inicia os pagamentos de outubro do Bolsa Família 2026 nesta segunda-feira (19). Os primeiros a receber serão os beneficiários com Número de Identificação Social (NIS) com final 1.

Este é o primeiro dia de pagamentos com os valores reajustados pelo governo. Anunciado em 17 de setembro , o aumento elevou o piso do Bolsa Família de R$ 600 para R$ 691 e também ampliou os benefícios complementares. (leia mais abaixo)

O dinheiro é disponibilizado nos últimos 10 dias úteis de cada mês, de forma escalonada. A exceção é o mês de dezembro, quando os pagamentos são antecipados.

🤔 Para saber a data correta de recebimento, a família deve verificar o último dígito do NIS , impresso no cartão do programa. Assim, é possível consultar o dia correspondente no calendário oficial de pagamentos.

Confira o calendário do Bolsa Família para outubro de 2026:

A previsão de pagamentos para os dois últimos meses do ano é:

Bolsa Família — Foto: Luis Lima Jr/FotoArena/Estadão Conteúdo

Veja abaixo perguntas e respostas sobre o Bolsa Família.

A principal regra para receber o benefício é ter renda mensal familiar de até R$ 218 por pessoa.

Para se enquadrar do programa, é preciso somar a renda total e dividir pelo número de pessoas. Caso o valor fique abaixo dos R$ 218 , a família está elegível ao Bolsa Família.

Os beneficiários também precisam arcar com contrapartidas, como:

manter crianças e adolescentes na escola;

fazer o acompanhamento pré-natal (no caso de gestantes);

manter as carteiras de vacinação atualizadas.

Com a mudança anunciada pelo governo , o Bolsa Família passou a prever o pagamento mínimo de R$ 691 por família.

A medida também elevou de R$ 142 para R$ 164 o chamado Benefício de Renda de Cidadania . Esse é o valor pago por integrante da família pelo programa.

🔎 Se uma família elegível tiver três pessoas , por exemplo, a soma será de R$ 492 (3 × R$ 164). Como o valor fica abaixo do piso, a família receberá o complemento necessário para chegar a R$ 691 .

🔎 Já uma família de cinco pessoas terá como base R$ 820 (5 × R$ 164).

Além do piso, há benefícios complementares, que também foram reajustados:

R$ 173 por criança de até 6 anos (eram R$ 150);

R$ 58 por criança ou adolescente de 7 a 17 anos (eram R$ 50);

R$ 58 por bebê de até 6 meses (eram R$ 50).

Na prática, portanto, o valor recebido por cada família varia conforme sua composição e pode aumentar com os benefícios adicionais para crianças, adolescentes e gestantes.

Os beneficiários precisam se inscrever no Cadastro Único (CadÚnico) — principal instrumento do governo federal para a inclusão de famílias de baixa renda em programas sociais — e aguardar uma análise de enquadramento.

Estar no Cadastro Único não significa a entrada automática nos programas sociais do governo, uma vez que cada um deles tem regras específicas. Mas o cadastro é pré-requisito para que a inscrição seja avaliada.

Os beneficiários recebem e podem movimentar os valores pelo aplicativo Caixa TEM e internet banking . Assim, não é necessário ir até uma agência da Caixa Econômica Federal — que é responsável pelo pagamento do Bolsa Família — para realizar o saque.

Segundo a Caixa, os beneficiários também podem utilizar o cartão do programa para realizar compras nos estabelecimentos comerciais, por meio da função de débito.

Além disso, há a opção de realizar saques nos terminais de autoatendimento, casas lotéricas e correspondentes Caixa Aqui, além das agências da Caixa.

articles.title: Batteries to autos: Chinese imports remain in top gear
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Every cheer for electric vehicle sales in the country also means that import of batteries from China goes up too given the complete dominance
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Every cheer for electric vehicle sales in the country also means that import of batteries from China goes up too given the complete dominance India’s neighbour enjoys in the global trade of this product.Not surprisingly, the spurt in the sale of EVs in India has resulted in import of batteries from across the border nearly doubling to $2.9 billion during April-Aug, making it the sixth largest import item from China so far this year, the latest commerce department data showed. The high growth has meant that it has overtaken electronic instruments, electric machinery, plastic raw materials and residual chemicals. With India and other countries failing to make any technological breakthrough, import of batteries is only going to surge. Indian battery makers, the few that have managed to set up shop after the PLI for the sector failed, in any case, are just packing the cells imported from China.There are other areas of concern too. For instance, two-and three-wheeler imports have shot up to $107 million during April-Aug, compared with $2 million a year ago. Similarly, car imports are up 2.6 times to $226 million in the first five months of FY27 -- probably led by BYD -- from $87 million in the corresponding period last year. Even gold and silver imports have surged as have oil products (3x to $179 million), dye intermediates (2.6x to $338 million) and bulk minerals (3x to $180 million) but they remain small compared with electronics, machinery, chemicals and plastics that make up around three-fourth of imports from China.With its firm grip over the electronics and telecom value chain, higher production of mobiles, computers and other devices in the India has not led to imports of components and inputs from China shrinking in any way. Official data showed that telecom equipment, including mobiles, as well as electronic components have seen over 40% imports growth in the first five months, when trade deficit with China widened to nearly $56 billion as against $44.7 billion during April-Aug 2025. At this pace, it is set to cross the deficit for 2025-26, which was pegged at $112 billion.No wonder, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman and commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal have expressed a worry about it in recent days and last week both underlined the need for a “fair deal”. While Indian exports have increased 40% this year, a bulk of it is inputs, and on a small base with average monthly exports remaining below $2 billion during April-Aug (see graphic).For India to replace Chinese goods is tough given the cost advantages that come with economies of scale in addition to subsidies that are doled out. China is unwilling to cede any ground. “If you look at the way China’s been developing, it’s different from the way Japan and Korea did, where they moved up the manufacturing ladder. China is filling the entire spectrum; they don’t appear to be releasing the lower end. That’s blocking the countries below them from doing what China did,” S&P global chief economist Paul Grunwald told TOI in a recent interview.“While we talk of trade deficit, if China turns off the tap, several of our industries including pharma, electronics machinery and chemicals, will be severely hit. We need to create domestic capacity across industries and deepen local manufacturing in these sectors,” said Ajay Srivastava, founder of trade think tank GTRI. articles.title: Bagchi to soon present HDFC Bank roadmap
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Anup Bagchi, who is set to take over as HDFC Bank’s managing director and CEO, said he would soon draw up a strategic roadmap covering growth,
articles.body: MUMBAI: Anup Bagchi, who is set to take over as HDFC Bank’s managing director and CEO, said he would soon draw up a strategic roadmap covering growth, margins, asset quality and productivity, as outgoing chief Sashidhar Jagdishan said the bank’s net interest margins (NIMs) had bottomed out and would improve from the next quarter.Speaking during the bank’s Q2 FY27 earnings call, Bagchi said he would consult regulators, customers, shareholders and other stakeholders before setting organisational priorities. He said the roadmap would focus on capital deployment, execution and governance as the bank responds to changes in the economy, artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. “The clear long-term goal is to deliver sustainable long-term value for shareholders, employees, and clients,” Bagchi said.Jagdishan, who is stepping down after six years at the helm, said margins had come under pressure because lending rates fell faster than the cost of deposits during the rate-cut cycle. He said the trend would reverse as the rate cycle turned and retail and MSME loans accounted for a larger share of the bank’s assets. “The trajectory will be upward from the next quarter on,” Jagdishan said, responding to a question on the outlook for margins.HDFC Bank on Saturday reported a 4.7% year-on-year increase in net profit to 19,510 crore in the July-Sept quarter of FY27 (Q2FY27), as a decline in other income and higher operating expenses and provisions partly offset growth in core interest income.With 70% of loans linked to floating rates, mostly to the repo, the Oct rate hike is expected to reprice much of the book by Dec. Of Rs 1.6 lakh crore in deposit growth, Rs 1.3 lakh crore came from time deposits and FCNR(B) inflows, offsetting gains from calling AT1 bonds in Aug.Jagdishan said the branch network doubled over five years and will support deposit growth as it matures. Repayment of Rs 2.6 lakh crore in inherited HDFC Ltd wholesale borrowings distorted headline figures, while retail CASA remained in the late 40s. Technology investments are beginning to cut turnaround times through automated processes. Employee numbers have stayed flat for three years, but the workforce will shift towards customer-facing roles, with headcount potentially rising in three to four years.Jagdishan announced that Bharucha, a 30-year veteran who helped build the bank’s credit architecture, had sought early retirement by Dec 31, 2026. Jagdishan also said his tenure had included regulatory restrictions, Covid, the HDFC Ltd merger and governance issues. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have withdrawn Rs 52,100 crore from Indian equities in Oct so far, as elevated crude oil prices, higher US bond yields and a stronger dollar weighed on investor sentiment. The latest outflow follows a net withdrawal of Rs 35,861 crore in Sept. FPIs had invested Rs 20,200 crore in Indian equities in July and Rs 29,631 crore in Aug, according to data from the Central Depository Services (CDSL).With the latest selling, cumulative FPI outflow from Indian equities in 2026 has reached over Rs 3.1 lakh crore, way higher than the Rs 1.7 lakh crore withdrawn during the entire 2025, the data showed.Dheeraj Gaur, chief investment strategy officer at Choice Wealth, said FPIs continued to sell Indian equities amid elevated US bond yields, a stronger dollar and rising crude oil prices. Sticky US inflation has also fuelled expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike, making US assets more attractive to foreign investors, he said. Meanwhile, expensive crude oil is adding to economic pressures in India, while the AI-led rally in North Asian markets is drawing foreign funds away from domestic equities, Gaur added.However, foreign investors turned marginal buyers on Oct 16. This brief reversal is likely to be tactical rather than indicative of a structural shift in investor sentiment.V K Vijayakumar, chief investment strategist at Geojit Investments, said the marginal decline in the US 10-year bond yield from above 5.3% to 5.08% and the rupee’s strengthening against the dollar were significant factors behind the temporary change in FPI stance.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Call for digital swaraj reflects need for greater data control’: IBM India chief Sandip Patel
articles.summary: MUMBAI: IBM India and South Asia managing director Sandip Patel said his call for “digital swaraj” reflects businesses’ and govts’ growing need to
articles.body: MUMBAI: IBM India and South Asia managing director Sandip Patel said his call for “digital swaraj” reflects businesses’ and govts’ growing need to exercise greater control over their data, technology assets and the systems that manage them.“I have started calling this the era of digital swaraj. In a predominantly digital world and a global digital economy, organisations need a degree of digital sovereignty suited to their level of regulation and the criticality of their operations,” Patel told TOI at its flagship event, IBM Think, held here.Geopolitical developments and regulatory requirements have heightened concerns over data sovereignty, particularly among organisations in regulated sectors such as banking.Companies increasingly want clarity on where their data resides and who controls encryption keys, where the control plane is located and whether compliance can be demonstrated continuously.IBM’s Sovereign Core, announced in March, is designed to address these concerns. The software stack can be deployed in a client or partner-owned data centre, providing cloud-like capabilities while keeping control-plane operations and key management within the customer’s jurisdiction.Built on Sovereign Core, IBM Bharat Core is an AI stack optimised for India, offering reusable Indic AI services, models and connectors across industries. It is benchmarked for quality and scale in Indian scenarios and guides users through the AI lifecycle by recommending suitable building blocks and infrastructure tailored to India’s requirements.IBM is also developing India-specific tools to accelerate Sovereign Core implementation, while its Svaiam reference architecture is designed to help deploy sovereign AI capabilities within govt environments. The shift towards greater control over technology infrastructure is also supporting India’s data centre growth. Patel identified two drivers: companies building capacity in India to support global operations, and Indian enterprises investing in infrastructure they can control themselves.IBM, MeitY Startup Hub to boost deep-tech venturesIBM and MeitY Startup Hub (MSH), an initiative of the ministry of electronics and information technology, plan to accelerate India’s deep-tech startup ecosystem by providing startups access to IBM’s technology expertise, mentorship, enterprise engagement opportunities and skilling programmes. Startups will get access to IBM’s enterprise technologies and innovation platforms to address business use cases. articles.summary: Oil prices fell on Monday as US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia raised the prospect of additional fuel supplies
articles.body: Oil prices fell on Monday as US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia raised the prospect of additional fuel supplies entering the market. However, continuing security threats in the Middle East and uncertainty over US-Iran negotiations kept the outlook for crude volatile.Brent crude declined $1.56, or 1.42%, to $108.3, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down 0.25, or 0.25%, at $101.2 a barrel.The previous week, US President Donald Trump had signed an executive order granting a waiver on key sanctions and tariffs imposed under the law known as the Graham Act. The legislation was signed last month after lawmakers urged the president to put pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.Secretary of state Marco Rubio said Trump would use up to 60 days to evaluate the economic consequences of the waiver.The move came after Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to export diesel to the US. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the US actions, saying they would hurt Ukraine.Brent crude had climbed to $110 a barrel briefly on Friday, marking its first such level since May, as mounting tensions in the Middle East heightened concerns about the security of shipping routes and the availability of global energy supplies.The pressure on supplies has been compounded by attacks on commercial vessels. Gulf crude flows fell to approximately 8.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average last week, down from more than 20 million barrels per day in the previous week, according to analytics firm Kpler. In a note issued on Friday, the firm also reported at least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels during the week.The risk of a wider regional confrontation remained in focus, with Egypt stating that it was prepared to offer Saudi Arabia the support required to protect its security and stability against Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.Despite Monday’s decline, crude markets face another week of potential price swings. Supply concerns across West Asia and stalled negotiations between the US and Iran are fuelling fears of further disruptions, while measures aimed at easing shortages are providing some relief, analysts said.Market participants will look to upcoming inventory figures for a clearer picture of supply and demand. The data under scrutiny include weekly crude stock estimates from the American Petroleum Institute (API), inventories at Cushing, total US oil stocks and crude imports.Developments around the Strait of Hormuz will also remain crucial to the market outlook. articles.title: ‘We are learning to live with weaker currency’: Arvind Panagariya
articles.summary: Columbia University professor and 16th Finance Commission chairman Arvind Panagariya, who was in India for the Kautilya Conclave, spoke to TOI, arguing
articles.body: Columbia University professor and 16th Finance Commission chairman Arvind Panagariya, who was in India for the Kautilya Conclave, spoke to TOI, arguing that a weaker rupee will not just make exports competitive but will also keep the prices of finished imported goods higher. In an interview, he suggested tariff cuts, doing away with quality control orders and revisiting bilateral investment treaties. Excerpts:Sitting in New York, how do you see the Indian economy evolving? What is the feedback that you’re getting from colleagues and investors?The general perception of the Indian economy is very positive. My assessment is that we will continue to grow at 7-8%. Manufacturinggrowth of 10% or so in the last three years gives me a lot of confidence; it is a very positive sign for the future. Inflation has remained stable, current account deficit has been very manageable. So, the vitals are all good.Given the headwinds due to west Asia in terms of higher cost, logistics, there is nervousness. Is that a big challenge?I don’t see our entrepreneurs nervous about growth prospects. Headwinds have been there and entrepreneurs have learnt to live with these things. We emerged very quickly and robustly from Covid. Our exports to the US and overall went up despite Trump’s tariffs, which shows that exporters have learnt to cope with this uncertainty. Finally, we seem to also be learning that currency depreciation is not always a bad thing. It is a very important change in our own attitudes. Indian products have to be competitive in the domestic market compared to imported goods.A big concern with a weaker rupee has been that import bill rises.The increase in the cost of imports basically tells you that our goods are more competitive relative to the foreign goods. The cost of my inputs rises, but the cost of the goods that are coming in to compete with my (finished) goods rises even more. Our exports did so well between 2000 and 2011 because the dollar appreciated against the rupee between 1991 and 2002 by 170%. But it stayed around that level till 2011 or so, actually the rupee appreciated in nominal terms, before weakening. As a result, after crossing $300 billion in 2011-12, it fell below that mark and only increased post-Covid.India has signed multiple trade agreements that reduce tariffs bilaterally. What else needs to be done?This is much needed and I also want the agreement with the US to go through as it will not only give us access, it will also lead to the opening up of our own markets, which is very much required. Several QCOs have been suspended but there are many more that need to be repealed because they are offering protection. The Bureau of Indian Standards does not have the staff to implement them domestically and the intent seems to be protectionist. India is also among the top users of anti-dumping duty. Anti-dumping is sometimes even more pernicious than tariffs because these duties can be very large and also very targeted as you go after your cheapest supplier.What about the bilateral investment treaty?We need to take a comprehensive look at the bilateral investment treaties because if we are going to attract foreign investors then we have to see what our competitors are doing, what China is doing, what Vietnam is doing.Do you see future American presidents weaponising tariffs the way Trump has done?The US commitment to WTO has certainly weakened. The current President has acted as if WTO really doesn’t matter. The only restraint on him has been domestic US laws and even that he has at times neglected. I doubt if future presidents will do like that. But what has happened permanently, and is something that was already underway, is the weakening of the WTO discipline. Subsidies were given, like through the Chips Act during the Biden administration, which was in violation of WTO rules. With the appellate body not functioning there is no way it can be addressed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: China economy grows thanks to AI export boom but domestic slump remains a drag
articles.summary: China reported better-than-expected Q3 growth on Monday as robust exports of chips and electronics components on the back of a global artificial intelligence boom buoy the world’s second-largest economy, despite sluggish demand at home.
articles.body: China reported better-than-expected Q3 growth on Monday as robust exports of chips and electronics components on the back of a global artificial intelligence boom buoy the world’s second-largest economy, despite sluggish demand at home. China’s National Bureau of Statistics said the economy grew 4.5% from a year earlier in the quarter ending September, a slight improvement from the more than three-year low of 4.3% last quarter and meeting the lower end of Beijing’s 4.5-5% annual target. This came as China has demonstrated its resilience in weathering the economic shocks of President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive – now on pause after both sides agreed to a truce – as well as the US’s war with Iran, which has dragged down growth in other nations. For the first nine months of 2026, the economy expanded 4.6%. The latest quarterly figure underscores the continuing challenge facing China’s leadership: the deepening imbalance that has made the country increasingly reliant on manufacturing and overseas markets. The phenomenon has come to be described by economists as a “two-speed economy”: a thriving export engine powered by high-tech manufacturing, alongside weak investment and stagnant domestic consumption. A prolonged housing market downturn, now in its fifth year, remains a drag, as an estimated 70% of Chinese household wealth is tied up in property. Property investment plunged 20.2% in the first three quarters of the year, indicating that the country’s real estate woes persist. Investment, a major pillar of the Chinese economy, was still weak, Monday’s figures showed. Fixed-asset investment, which includes spending on infrastructure, factories and property, fell 7.2% in the first nine months of the year from the same period in 2025, declining at the same pace as the first eight months, according to data released on Monday. However, retail sales, a key gauge of consumption, saw a remarkable turnaround, growing 1.1% in September, an improvement from the modest 0.4% increase in August and the fastest growth since March. “The economy moved forward under pressure and developed in a newer and better direction, with an increase in positive changes in key indicators,” said Mao Shengyong, vice-minister of the National Bureau of Statistics, at a Monday press conference. “At the same time, we must also recognize that the international environment is complex and volatile, the problem of insufficient domestic demand remains relatively prominent, and the foundation for the steady and positive growth of the economy still needs to be consolidated,” he added. Beijing has made expanding domestic demand a top priority for 2026. Last month, the government unveiled a mix of limited stimulus measures, including mortgage subsidies for first-time home buyers and targeted rate cuts, after the cabinet pledged to step up support to meet its annual growth target. But more support may be needed if the momentum fails to sustain into the fourth quarter, economists say. Last week, the IMF downgraded its growth forecast for China this year from 4.6% to 4.5%, citing persistent weakness in domestic demand. It also revised down its 2027 projection for China from 4.1% to 4%. “Sluggishness in domestic consumption and weakening investment amid continued property sector strains were only partly offset by robust export performance,” the IMF said in its latest global growth outlook report. Meanwhile, the financial organization upgraded its global economy growth forecast this year from 3.0% to 3.1%. Strong exports Trade remained the main engine for the Chinese economy over the third quarter, paving the way for the country to reach a new record in trade surplus this year. China’s exports surged 36.3% last month from a year earlier, marking the biggest jump since early 2021, according to the latest data released from the country’s customs last week. Exports to the United States also jumped 39.6% year-on-year in September. AI-related exports and green-tech products like batteries drove the bulk of the export boom, contributing to $938.1 billion in trade surplus for the first nine months of the year, compared to $875.1 billion the same period in 2025. While exports from the world’s factory have increasingly drawn the ire of countries around the world, Beijing has managed so far to calm trade tensions with major trading partners, such as the US and the European Union. At their summit last month, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump secured an extension of their trade truce to January next year, and agreed to tariff reductions on $60 billion worth of goods. The two are expected to meet again in November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Beijing and Brussels also reached an initial agreement on trade this month, including capping China’s hybrid vehicle exports to the EU and improving market access, narrowly avoiding an all-out trade war between the country and the bloc. But the agreement could also dent the booming auto export, experts said.

articles.title: Anthropic says it will commit 5% of shares to ‘public benefit’ fund
articles.summary: Claude creator says fund could be used for donations to NGOs and ‘direct distributions to specific populations’.
articles.body:
Anthropic has pledged to commit 5 percent of its shares to a new fund dedicated to the public good, with plans to increase the contribution as the artificial intelligence giant’s market value grows.

The creator of the AI assistant Claude announced the new “Anthropic Public Benefit Fund” on Sunday as tech firms face intense scrutiny over the potential dangers posed by the frontier technology.

In a blog post, Anthropic said it was committing 5 percent of company shares with immediate effect, subject to stockholder approval, with an additional 2 percent to be added “at the board’s discretion” for every 50 percent increase in the company’s value.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the San Francisco-based firm said.

“It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.”

Anthropic said the fund could be used to make donations to traditional nonprofits, as well as “direct distributions to specific populations”.

It said labour market disruption due to AI could be among the causes addressed by the fund.

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said.

“The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic, officially registered as a “public benefit corporation” in the US state of Delaware, said the fund would not be used for lobbying or political donations, either in the United States or overseas.

Founded in 2021 by former employees of ChatGPT creator OpenAI, Anthropic is preparing for what could be the largest public initial offering in history. It is expected to list on the US stock market before the end of 2026, with analysts forecasting a valuation exceeding $2 trillion.

The company’s charter requires its leadership to balance shareholder returns with responsible AI development.

The breakneck speed of AI development has prompted widespread anxiety about possible negative downstream effects on society, including the job market.

In a report published last month, consulting firm McKinsey estimated that up to 11 million American workers may need to switch careers over the next decade due to AI-driven automation.

articles.title: Homebuyers paid Rs 2.06 crore but got no flat, builder said payments meant accepting delay; Bombay HC orders interest payout from 2017 saying RERA allows for unconditional right to monthly interest
articles.summary: What happens if the possession of your dream home is delayed?
articles.body: What happens if the possession of your dream home is delayed? You buy an apartment, sign an agreement, make the necessary payments, but the builder repeatedly fails to deliver the flat on time. Are you entitled to interest payout under RERA Act?In one such case, the Bombay High Court has ordered the builder to pay interest and ruled that buyers have an unconditional right to monthly interest in case of project delays.What the case is aboutTwo homebuyers filed a case against the builder. The dispute concerned an apartment for which they had signed the sale agreement in 2014, with possession due by June 30, 2017.The flat's consideration was Rs 1.95 crore. By the time of the complaint, the buyers had paid Rs 2.06 crore, including the consideration paid to the promoter, stamp duty, registration charges and applicable taxes.Also Read | US-based daughter files case against parents seeking share in properties; Karnataka HC rejects her ‘ancestral’ claim, saying they were father's separate assets, not coparcenary propertyHowever, when they didn’t get the possession by the agreed deadline, the buyers approached MahaRERA, seeking possession along with interest for the delay. In January 2019, the authority directed the developer to hand over the apartment with an occupancy certificate by December 31, 2019, while allowing the buyers to seek interest at a later stage.The buyers appealed. In March 2021, the Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal directed the promoter to pay interest at the State Bank of India's highest marginal cost of lending rate plus 2% on the amount paid, from July 1, 2017, until possession was handed over. It also awarded Rs 25,000 in costs.The builder challenged that order before the Bombay High Court. The developer's argument was that by continuing to pay installments under revised schedules, and by not objecting to its letters announcing new dates, the buyers had in effect accepted the delay.The promoter relied on Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, which addresses the consequences of accepting delayed contractual performance without notifying the other party of an intention to claim compensation.The developer also invoked contractual force majeure provisions and the COVID-19 pandemic.Also Read | Grandmother and her son gifted 2.5-acre land to his second wife, who sold it; his daughter from first marriage claimed it was ancestral, but Madras HC rejects her pleaWhy did the court rule in favour of homebuyers?According to Gaurav Dasgupta, Partner, Khaitan & Co, this is one of the most homebuyer-friendly rulings he has seen this year.Its message is simple: a developer cannot turn a buyer's patience into a waiver.The Bombay High Court examined whether accepting delayed performance could deprive homebuyers of their right to interest under Section 18 of RERA. It held that the statutory protection could not be made conditional on giving the notice contemplated under Section 55 of the Contract Act.The Bombay High Court rejected this since RERA is a special act for real estate, which overrides a general act like contract act, when there is a conflict between the provisions.“It held that Section 18 of RERA gives a buyer who stays with a delayed project an unconditional right to monthly interest. Following the Supreme Court, it said that right cannot be cut down by conditions or by events the buyer does not control. RERA is a beneficial legislation, and the court upheld the spirit of the act,” explains Gaurav Dasgupta.Also Read | Man enters JDA for land, gets 6 flats from builder and transfers 5 to wife, but gets tax notice; ITAT Delhi deletes Rs 4.14 crore additions after finding no stock-in-trade conversion or saleThe developer's letters were information, not a renegotiation, according to the court.“A new date cannot be agreed informally by conduct, and in an ongoing RERA project the only lawful way to extend time is to extend the registration with the regulator after following due process of law. The Court also refused to let the developer rely on Covid-19, because the pandemic came long after the 2017 deadline had already passed,” Dasgupta tells TOI.In earlier similar cases, the court had given a ruling about payment of interest from the advent of RERA, but in this case, the court went on to uphold the allowing of interest from the date of original possession, even though it was before RERA came into force.The court dismissed the builder’s appeal which argued that the buyers had accepted changes to the possession schedule and could not subsequently claim interest without giving the developer notice. The High Court held that Section 18 of RERA protects a buyer's right to interest for delayed possession, even when the buyer chooses to remain in the project.Explaining the purpose of the legislation, the court said RERA was enacted “to protect the interest of consumer in the real estate sector”. It then clarified the right available to buyers who decide not to withdraw from a delayed project.The court held that Section 18 gives buyers an “unqualified absolute right” to accept delayed performance without giving up their claim to interest for every month of delay.Also Read | He bought a diesel SUV for Rs 13.69 lakh; but repeated DPF issues followed; consumer commission finds deficiency in service and awards Rs 10.99 lakh refund, 9% interest and compensationThe promoter had argued that the buyers' conduct showed acceptance of revised possession dates. However, the High Court noted that the appellate tribunal had found “no authentic evidence” that they had accepted the revised possession date or waived their right to interest.The court also examined the developer's communications. It observed that these primarily informed buyers about the delay and offered assurances about completion. As the judgment states, “The revised timelines are couched in a manner so as to be in nature of information requiring no further acts by the allottees.”Importantly, the court held that even if the buyers had accepted the revised date, that would not extinguish their statutory entitlement. It stated: “Even accepting that there was acceptance of revised date of possession, considering Section 18 of RERA Act, the allottees were well within their rights to accept the delayed performance without foregoing their right to interest for delayed possession.”On the pandemic defence, the court noted that the contractual deadline was June 2017 and the project's revised completion date under RERA registration was December 2019. COVID-19 came later and, the court held, “does not impact the performance of the contract.”The Bombay High Court therefore upheld the direction to pay interest from July 1, 2017, until possession was handed over, and dismissed the promoter's second appeal on June 18, 2026.Significance of rulingAccording to Gaurav Dasgupta, for homebuyers, paying installments on time while a project runs late does not cost you your interest claim.“Thus, it is important to keep faith in RERA and not violate any provisions of payment as agreed in the project timeline and then seek legal recourse for any violation on the part of the developer, including interest and costs,” he says.For developers, the lesson is just as clear.“If timelines slip, the answer is a formal extension under RERA, not reassuring letters to buyers. Interest liability starts on the contractual date and keeps running unless the extension is expressly agreed under the due process established under RERA – getting approval of 2/3rd of the allottees and approval of RERA,” he adds.It’s important to note that the ruling has been challenged before the Supreme Court through a special leave petition filed on 24 July 2026.The developer’s advocate had initially said that an out-of-court settlement was being explored, but later stated that they want full-fledged hearing in the appeal, says Dasgupta.The question the Supreme Court may now have to answer is whether this long-established Contract Act rule has any role left in RERA disputes.You use AI every day.
